sens: Gift or sacrifice presented to God and burned on the altar
Fatty part or food burned as a pleasing offering
Right of the priest to consume certain offerings
Whole of the sacrificial worship and its rituals
H0801.detail:
1. The offering consumed by fire is a gift brought to God and entirely or partially burned on the altar to please and honor Him. In Exodus 29:18, the whole ram becomes a burnt offering, "a sacrifice consumed by fire, of a pleasing aroma to the Lord": the smoke that rises is like the fragrance of the gift that reaches God. It is an act of worship and consecration.
2. Often, it is not the whole animal that burns, but its most precious fatty parts, the first to be burned before the Lord (Leviticus 3:3-5, 9-11, 14-16). What goes up in flames is what has the most value, offered to God alone, and that is what "ascends" to Him: the image is that of the sacrifice that "rises" to heaven.
3. Some offerings consumed by fire become food for the priests: they eat the leftovers after a portion has burned (Leviticus 10:13). The priest has an established right to it, a holy portion, signifying that God nourishes those who serve Him.
4. The expression also refers to the whole sacrificial system and the rules that accompany it. In Leviticus 21:6 and Deuteronomy 18:1, the priests are "those who offer to the Lord the sacrifices consumed by fire": this is their central function, what defines them.
H0801.origine: The Hebrew word אִשֶּׁה (ishshah) likely comes from a root meaning "fire" or "to burn," related to verbs of combustion. The initial image is that of fire consuming, of the flame rising. It is a specifically cultic word, rarely used outside the context of sacrifice, which shows how central the idea of burning before God was in Israel's thought.
H0801.emploi: The word appears 64 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively in the books of law: Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, and a few mentions in Joshua and Samuel. It is the technical term for Israelite sacrificial worship. In Leviticus 1-7, which describes the different types of sacrifices, it is applied to the burnt offering (which burns entirely: Leviticus 1:9, 13, 17), to the grain offering of which certain parts burn (Leviticus 2:2-3, 9-11, 16), to the thank offerings of which the fatty parts are burned (Leviticus 3:3-16). In Numbers 28-29, it refers to the daily sacrifices and festivals: each day, offerings are made to the Lord "of sacrifices consumed by fire." The word can designate the entirety of an offering (when everything burns) or only the burned part (when the rest is eaten). It is an act of regular and perpetual worship.
H0801.portee: This offering teaches the believer that worshiping God means giving Him the best we have, what truly costs us, and that this gift is not for our use but entirely for Him. The fire that consumes is a sign that nothing returns to the giver: it is an act of faith and voluntary relinquishment. For Israel, offering "the offering consumed by fire" was the expression of the indestructible bond with God, renewed each day. Although the sacrificial system is fulfilled in Jesus Christ, this word reminds us that true worship requires the gift of oneself, not half-measures.

sens: Person of the female sex, as opposed to man
Married woman, wife of a man
Female of an animal
Each, anyone (pronominal use)
H0802G.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a woman as a human being of the female sex. In Genesis 2:22, God forms the woman from the rib of the man and brings her to him: this is the origin of the distinction between man and woman in creation. In Judges 9:51, men and women are mentioned who take refuge in a tower, showing that the term designates the female half of humanity.
2. The word also designates the wife, the married woman. A woman engaged or married to a man is called his wife (Leviticus 19:20). Marriage unites a man and a woman in a recognized couple relationship.
3. The word also applies to female animals: a heifer or a female beast can be called woman in the Hebrew text, just as one would refer to the male of a species.
4. Rarely, the word takes on a general or pronominal value: "each, anyone" in certain contexts where one wants to speak of an indeterminate person, man or woman.
H0802G.origine: The Hebrew word isha (woman) comes from a root that evokes existence and vitality. It is linked to ish (man), and together these two terms mark the fundamental distinction between the sexes in creation. The word is very ancient and belongs to the basic vocabulary of Hebrew. It has no clear cognates in other Semitic languages, but its meaning has been stable from the beginning to the end of the Bible.
H0802G.emploi: The word appears 297 times in the Old Testament, especially in Genesis, Leviticus, and the historical books. It is used to speak of women in all contexts of life: creation, marriage, family, worship, law. In Genesis 2-3, it designates Eve and her role in creation and the fall. Leviticus often uses it in laws about purity and sexual relations. The historical books speak of remarkable women (Deborah, Bathsheba, the widow of Zarephath) or everyday situations. The word can also designate a woman in her social function: slave, fiancée, widow. Sometimes it takes on a pejorative connotation, as in Ecclesiastes 7:26 where the woman becomes the image of seduction and the trap.
H0802G.portee: This word lays the foundations for the dignity of women in the Bible. Created in the image of God just like man, the woman is not an inferior creature, but equal to man in her nature. Biblical narratives show strong, faithful, and wise women. However, the role of women in the original sin and its consequences also reminds us of human vulnerability and the need for salvation. For the believer, recognizing the true status of women in God's plan — creation, companion, mother, prophetess — is a matter of faithfulness to the Word.

sens: female person, as opposed to man
wife, married woman to a man
female, in animals
each one (pronoun usage)
H0802H.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a woman as a person, defined by her female sex — the other half of humanity. This is clearly seen in Genesis 2:24, where the woman is distinguished from the man, and together they form the human couple. This is the broadest sense, which includes all others.

2. More often, "woman" means "wife," the woman united to a man by marriage. Genesis 24:67 illustrates this well: Isaac "took Rebekah, she became his wife," marking the marital union. It is in this sense that the Law forbids uncovering the nakedness of a brother's wife (Leviticus 18:16), or that the king commands, "Whoever touches his wife shall be put to death" (Genesis 26:11).

3. The word also applies to females in the animal world. Genesis 7:2 commands to take "of every kind of clean animals, the male and its female," to save them from the flood. This is a natural extension of the same word.

4. Rarely, "woman" functions as an indefinite pronoun, each, especially in the plural. This nuance is more subtle in the provided usages.
H0802H.origine: The Hebrew word אִשָּׁה (ishshah) is formed from the root אִישׁ (ish), which means "man" or "person." According to rabbinic tradition, ishshah evokes the idea of "she who is of man" or "she who comes from man," alluding to the creation of Eve taken from Adam's rib (Genesis 2:22-23). The word has a feminine grammatical structure that emphasizes this distinction of sex. In Hebrew, it is one of the most common words for speaking of women in all their roles.
H0802H.emploi: The word appears 392 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost always to designate a woman or a wife. It is ubiquitous from Genesis, where we see Abraham with his wife Sarai (Genesis 12:5, 12:11), Isaac with Rebekah (Genesis 24:67), Jacob with his wives (Genesis 29:21, 29:28). The Mosaic Law uses it to specify kinship ties and sexual prohibitions (Leviticus 18:16). In historical narratives, it designates the wives of kings and leaders (1 Kings 2:21). The context shows that "woman" can be the wife of an ordinary man as well as that of a king, and that the marital relationship — union, fidelity, procreation — is its main horizon. Ezra 10:11 uses it in the plural for the "foreign wives" that the repatriated Jews must send away, showing that the status of woman is linked to the identity and covenant of the people.
H0802H.portee: This word reminds us that a woman is a complete person, created in the image of God (Genesis 1:27), and not a mere object. The marital covenant, where man and woman "become one flesh" (Genesis 2:24), is at the heart of God's plan for humanity. Understanding this term helps the modern reader grasp how the Bible honors women as companions of men, mothers of generations, and actors in the story of salvation.

sens: Each person or thing in a group, considered individually
All together, taken collectively
Each one (feminine, when speaking of women or creatures)
Every creature or object without exception
H0802I.detail:
1. The word designates a unique person or thing in a group, viewed separately from others: it conveys the idea of "each one taken individually." In Ruth 1:8, Naomi says to her two daughters-in-law: "Return each one to her mother's house," each taking her own path, alone.
2. Sometimes the word expresses the entirety of a group considered in its unity: "all together." In Exodus 26:3, the five curtains are "joined together," united with one another to form a coherent whole.
3. When the text speaks of women or female creatures, the word takes a feminine form: "each one." In Amos 4:3, the prophecy threatens the women of Samaria who will go out "each one before herself" through the breaches of the walls. Jeremiah 9:20 calls on women to learn mournful songs "from one another." 
4. The word can also simply mean "all without exception": in Isaiah 34:15, "all the vultures" will gather, each finding its place in this desolate place.
H0802I.origine: It is a form of the Hebrew word for "woman" or "wife" — an ancient root primarily designating the human being of female sex. Here, the word retains this root but has developed a broader and more abstract meaning: no longer "woman" as such, but the idea of individuality, distinction within a whole. This is a natural shift in Hebrew: from the concrete (a woman, several women) to the abstract (each one, one and another). This same root appears in other forms of Hebrew vocabulary related to personality and identity.
H0802I.emploi: This word appears 14 times in the provided biblical texts, mainly in the historical and prophetic books. In Exodus 26 (verses 3, 5, 6, 17), it describes the tabernacle curtains "joined together" — the image is that of distinct pieces united into a whole. In Ruth 1:8-9, it individualizes two women: each must return to her maternal home. In the prophets (Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Amos, Zechariah), the word serves to show that each person or creature acts or suffers judgment personally, without collective escape: the women of Samaria will go out "each one before herself." This shift between "together" and "each one" demonstrates the flexibility of Hebrew: the same word can unite or particularize depending on the context.
H0802I.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us of two truths that balance each other: the importance of community (we are "together") and that of personal responsibility (we are also "each one" before God). When God speaks through the prophets of judgment or salvation, He addresses specific individuals, not an anonymous crowd. Each one matters, each one responds personally.

sens: Base, underground structure on which a building rests
That which supports, that which keeps upright
Figuratively, that which ensures the stability and solidity of a reality
H0803.detail:
1. The foundation is the base built in the ground on which the entire building rests. It is the deep and hidden structure that holds and bears the weight of the entire edifice. In Jeremiah 50:15, the foundations of Babylon "collapse" when the city is besieged: without this base, the walls cannot stand.
2. More broadly, the foundation is that which supports and maintains something in stability. It is the support, the base on which everything rests. A construction without solid foundations inevitably collapses.
3. Figuratively, the word designates that which ensures the stability of a moral or spiritual reality: faith, wisdom, or a divine promise can be the foundation on which one builds their life.
H0803.origine: The Hebrew word אָשְׁיָה comes from a root that means "to support" or "to uphold." Its Aramaic equivalent אֹשׁ (osh) reinforces this sense of "foundation." The family of this word includes terms that evoke stable support and constructive solidity.
H0803.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Jeremiah 50:15, at the moment when the prophet announces the ruin of great Babylon. It precisely describes the material collapse of the city: its foundations collapse, leading to the downfall of its walls. This usage is clearly concrete and architectural, but it participates in a symbolic divine judgment where physical destruction is the visible sign of punishment.
H0803.portee: This word reminds us that all solidity, all apparent permanence, depends on a deep and often invisible foundation. For the believer, it invites examination of what foundations he builds upon: is the Word of God the unshakeable base of his life, or does he rely on human supports destined to collapse? The image of collapsing foundations shows that even what seems the strongest and most eternal can be overturned by God's judgment.

sens: Empire and political power dominating the ancient Near East
Geographical territory and region of the ancient Near East
Feared military power that conquers and deports peoples
Existential threat to the kingdom of Judah
Instrument of divine judgment on Israel
H0804G.detail:
1. Assyria is the political and military empire that dominates the Near East from the 9th to the 7th century BCE. It is mentioned as early as Genesis (2:14) to geographically situate the Tigris to the east of Assyria, establishing the ancient geographical context.

2. It is a region of the Near East, that of the upper Tigris and its tributaries, with its major cities like Nineveh. It occupies a strategic territory in Mesopotamia.

3. Assyria is known for its formidable military power: it conquers the Northern Kingdom (Israel) in 722 BCE, deports ten tribes (2 Kings 17:5-6), and constantly threatens Judah. It captures Samaria after a three-year siege (2 Kings 18:9-11).

4. For Judah in the 7th century, Assyria represents a vital threat. King Hezekiah pays it tribute (2 Kings 18:14-16) and implores divine deliverance (2 Kings 20:6) when the king of Assyria besieges him.

5. The prophets present Assyria as the rod of divine judgment: God uses it to correct His people (Isaiah 10:5), but it will itself be judged and broken when its role is fulfilled (Isaiah 14:25).
H0804G.origine: The name literally means "a step" or "a march" in its root. It designates the people and the empire of Ashur, the main god of this civilization. In Hebrew, the word can also be written as Asshur. Historical Assyria extends from the 2nd to the 7th century BCE and becomes a regional superpower under the Neo-Assyrian dynasty.
H0804G.emploi: The word appears 136 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the historical accounts of the Kings and Chronicles, and abundantly in the prophecies of Isaiah and Jeremiah. It primarily designates the political and military power: Shalmaneser and his successors conquer the territory of Israel and deport its population (2 Kings 17-19). The term is then used to speak of threats against Judah: the king of Assyria besieges Jerusalem and claims dominion over Judah (2 Kings 18-19 and parallels in 2 Chronicles 32). Finally, the prophets use it as an illustration of divine judgment: the Lord will whistle for "the bees that are in the land of Assyria" to send them as a plague (Isaiah 7:18), and Assyria itself will be broken when its mission of punishment is complete.
H0804G.portee: Understanding the role of Assyria in the Bible helps the believer see how God governs the history of nations and even uses wicked powers to fulfill His purpose of correction towards His people. The fate of Israel under Assyrian domination teaches that disobedience to God leads to captivity, while faith in God (like that of Hezekiah) brings deliverance. It is a reminder that divine judgment is real, but divine mercy can intervene for those who turn to Him.

sens: Son of Shem, ancestor of the Assyrians
The Assyrian people
The nation of Assyria
The territory of Assyria or the Assyrian empire
H0804H.detail:
1. Asshur is primarily the name of a man, the second son of Shem (the eldest son of Noah) according to Genesis 10:22. He lived during the time of the Patriarchs and is presented as the eponymous ancestor of the Assyrians — that is, the Assyrian people derived their name and origin from this founding figure.

2. The name Asshur also designates the Assyrian people themselves, the descendants of this historical ancestor, who formed a powerful civilization in Mesopotamia.

3. Asshur can also refer to the nation of Assyria as a political and military entity — the kingdom with its kings, laws, and armies.

4. The term finally applies to the territory or the Assyrian empire, the vast domain controlled by this power of the ancient Near East.
H0804H.origine: The name Asshur literally means "a march" or "a step," an image that perhaps evokes the founder walking toward a new land. It is a proper name derived from the genealogical tradition of Genesis, where the ancestors of the major peoples of the ancient world are listed according to their descent from Noah through his three sons. Asshur, son of Shem, occupies a key place in this genealogy, just like his brothers Elam, Arphaxad, Lud, and Aram, each giving their name to a people or region.
H0804H.emploi: Asshur appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, both times in genealogical lists: in Genesis 10:22 and in 1 Chronicles 1:17, where he is listed among the sons of Shem. These passages establish the genealogical link between the historical figure and the Assyrian people who would populate northern Mesopotamia. Although the name appears infrequently in the Bible, the people and empire of Assyria play a significant role in biblical history, particularly in the accounts of the kingdoms of Israel and Judah during the Assyrian and post-Assyrian periods.
H0804H.portee: Asshur reminds the reader that the Assyrian empire, so powerful and often threatening to the people of Israel, is not an autonomous and eternal force, but a human people with genealogy and origin like others — descended from the son of a distant ancestor. This situates biblical history within the broader context of the nations of the world, all linked to Noah and the providence of God.

sens: tribe descended from Abraham and Keturah through Jokshan and Dedan
H0805A.detail: The Ashurim are a tribe mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when the author lists the descendants of Abraham and his wife Keturah. Jokshan, son of Keturah, had several sons, including Dedan; from Dedan came three peoples: the Ashurim, the Letushim, and the Leummim (Genesis 25:3). These names designate ethnic groups or clans, probably peoples of the Middle East or Arabia, although few historical details are provided in the biblical text.
H0805A.origine: The name Ashurim may be related to Asshur, a figure or ancestor from the time of the Patriarchs, or derive from a root meaning "guided" or "blessed." It is a name of a people belonging to the Abrahamic genealogy.
H0805A.emploi: The Ashurim appear only once in the Bible, in Genesis 25:3, in the genealogical list of the children of Abraham. This passage, which enumerates the descendants of Keturah after Sarah's death, shows how the Bible connects various ancient peoples to the lineage of Abraham. Like the other peoples mentioned in this genealogy (Midianites, Sabeans, Dejanites), the Ashurim represent a distant people whose precise historical identity largely escapes us.

sens: Inhabitant of the tribe of Asher during the time of the Patriarchs
Member of the people settled in the region of Jezreel
H0805B.detail:
1. The Geshurite is a descendant of Asher, son of Israel and Zilpah. He is a member of the patriarchal tribe founded by this ancestor, mentioned from his birth in Genesis 30:13.
2. At the time of Abner and the division of the kingdom after the death of Saul, the Geshurites constitute a recognized population in the region of Jezreel, a fertile plain in northern Israel. It is in this context that 2 Samuel 2:9 mentions them as one of the populations under the authority of Ish-Bosheth, the son of Saul.
H0805B.origine: The word comes from the name Asher (אָשֵׁר), which means "guided" or "happy." Asher is one of the twelve sons of Israel (Jacob), born of Zilpah, Leah's maid. The suffix "-ite" marks tribal belonging: it designates someone who belongs to the tribe of Asher, just as "Judean" comes from Judah.
H0805B.emploi: The term "Geshurite" appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Samuel 2:9, during the account of the battles between Abner (commander of Saul) and David after Saul's death. Abner establishes Ish-Bosheth, son of Saul, as king and asserts his power over several regions, including that of the Geshurites. This mention situates the tribe of Asher as an identified and organized population in northern Israel.
H0805B.portee: This mention reminds us that each of the twelve tribes of Israel had its own history, territory, and role in the people of God. It also illustrates how, even in political struggles and civil wars, the different regions and peoples of Israel are recognized and named.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah at the time of Egypt and the desert
Son of Hezron and Abijah
Father of Tekoa and founder of its lineage
H0806.detail:
1. Aschchur is a man of the tribe of Judah mentioned at the time when Israel is leaving Egypt and crossing the desert (1 Chronicles 2:24). His name means "black" in Hebrew.
2. He is the son of Hezron and Abijah. He has half-brothers: Ram, Jerahmeel, Caleb, and Segub, all from Hezron by different mothers.
3. Aschchur is the "father of Tekoa" (1 Chronicles 2:24, 4:5), which means he founded or is the ancestor of a city or region called Tekoa. He has two wives, Helea and Naara, and several children who will form his descendants.
H0806.origine: The name Aschchur comes from a Hebrew root meaning "black." This type of descriptive name was common in the Old Testament, often reflecting a physical characteristic or a circumstance of birth. Aschchur belongs to the genealogy of Judah, one of the great tribes of Israel.
H0806.emploi: Aschchur appears only twice in the Bible, both in 1 Chronicles (2:24 and 4:5). He is presented as an important link in the genealogy of Judah: he first appears as the son of Hezron and Abijah, then as the father of Tekoa. These two verses complete the same event in his life: his married life with his two wives and his role as the founder of an important lineage. His name appears in genealogical lists that establish the family and territorial connections of the tribe of Judah.

sens: deity worshiped in Hamath
H0807.detail: Aschima is a deity, that is, a god or goddess, that the inhabitants of Hamath (a major city in northern Syria) honored and worshiped in ancient times. The Bible mentions it only once, in 2 Kings 17:30, in a passage that lists the false deities that various peoples deported to Assyria brought with them and continued to venerate.
H0807.origine: The name Aschima comes from the Hebrew אֲשִׁימָא. Its exact etymology remains uncertain, but the ancient definition links it to the idea of guilt or desolation. It was a deity of the Syrian pantheon, particularly venerated in Hamath, an important city in the Orontes Valley. No additional details about this deity are known from the Bible.
H0807.emploi: Aschima appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Kings 17:30. This verse reports that during the massive deportation of Israel to Assyria, the Assyrian authorities populated the northern kingdom with foreigners from various regions — Babylon, Cuth, Hamath, and others. Each of these peoples brought their own gods and continued to worship them in the land of Israel. Aschima is among these imported false deities, alongside Succoth-Benoth, Nergal, and others, testifying to the multiplicity of idolatrous cults that then established themselves in Samaria.

sens: Cake or bread made with pressed raisins
Comforting and strengthening food, used to support or fortify
Figuratively: that which diverts from the true God and His love
H0809.detail:
1. A raisin cake is a bread or pastry made from compressed raisins, solid and nourishing. It was a common food in Israel and the Middle East, easy to preserve and transport. King David distributes it to all the people during a celebration (2 Samuel 6:19): it is a festive dish.
2. This cake also served to restore and fortify the one who ate it. In the Song of Solomon (2:5), the speaker asks to be supported with raisin cakes and apples, as if this food had the power to uplift strength and courage. It is a remedy for discouragement.
3. Hosea uses it figuratively: the children of Israel love "raisin cakes," meaning they turn to other gods and the pleasures they offer instead of loving the Lord. The cake then becomes the image of everything that seduces and diverts from the true God. In Isaiah 16:7, "sighing over" evokes mourning and lamentation in the face of ruins — this is a derived meaning of the same word, expressing sorrow.
H0809.origine: The Hebrew word אֲשִׁישָׁה (ashishah) literally means a pressed or compacted thing — it comes from a root that means "to press" or "to compress." The raisins were indeed pressed together to form a solid cake. This word has no exact equivalent in Greek, and ancient translations have interpreted it in various ways depending on the context: sometimes as "cake," sometimes as "flask of wine" when thinking of a product of fermented grape.
H0809.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the Old Testament. Around the time of David and in Chronicles, it refers to a festive food distributed to the people (2 Samuel 6:19; 1 Chronicles 16:3). In the poetry of the Song of Solomon and among the prophets Isaiah and Hosea, its meaning becomes richer: it is what fortifies or seduces, what is good to taste but can lead away from true good. The context shows a progression from the concrete meaning (food) to the figurative meaning (spiritual seduction).
H0809.portee: This word reminds us that the Lord provides for all the needs of the people, even the small pleasures of the table and feast. But Hosea warns us: the pleasures of this world, even legitimate in themselves, become dangerous if they divert us from love for God. It is an invitation to keep our hearts set on the Lord rather than on what seduces our senses.

sens: External male reproductive organ
(Figuratively) Male strength, virility
H0810.detail:
1. The testicle is the male reproductive organ. In the Bible, the word appears in Leviticus 21:20 to refer to crushed or damaged testicles: it is a physical infirmity that, according to the law of Moses, rendered a priest unfit for service in the sanctuary.
2. The word can figuratively evoke strength, male power, or the ability to reproduce, although this figurative sense is not strongly marked in the preserved biblical texts.
H0810.origine: The Hebrew word אֶשֶׁךְ (eshekh) specifically refers to the testicle. It comes from a root that expresses the idea of firmness or hardness, which suits the nature of this organ. No other biblical word shares exactly this root, making this term quite isolated in Hebrew vocabulary.
H0810.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Leviticus 21:20. It is listed among the physical infirmities that exclude a man from the priesthood: a priest with crushed or damaged testicles could not approach the altar to offer sacrifices. This stipulation was part of the code of holiness and purity that God imposed on His priests. The context is strictly legal and medical.
H0810.portee: This passage reminds us that in the Old Testament, physical integrity was a sign of cultic purity. For the Christian today, this underscores the perfection of Jesus Christ, the Great Priest, who possesses the fullness of holiness. This text also invites us to look beyond visible infirmities: God's grace does not depend on our appearance or physical integrity.

sens: Group of fruits attached together on the same stem
Poetic image of what is sweet, attractive, or desirable
Sign of fertility and abundance
H0811.detail:
1. The bunch is primarily a collection of grapes attached to the same vine branch: it is the characteristic fruit of the vine in the Holy Land. In Numbers 13:23, the explorers cut a bunch so enormous that they carry it between two of them using a pole, thus demonstrating the abundance of the promised land.
2. The word becomes a poetic image to speak of what is beautiful and attractive. In Song of Solomon 1:14, the beloved is compared to a bunch of henna, expressing his sweetness and charm. Similarly, in 7:8, the breasts of the beloved are likened to bunches, celebrating the beauty of the body.
3. The bunch also symbolizes fertility and divine judgment. In Deuteronomy 32:32, the bitter bunches of Sodom and Gomorrah become a symbol of moral degeneration, while in Isaiah 65:8 the healthy bunch represents the faithful people that God preserves.
H0811.origine: The Hebrew word eshkol comes from a root that evokes the idea of "gathering" or "grouping." It naturally designates these fruits gathered on the same branch. In Numbers 13:24, the valley itself is named Eshcol (Nahal Eshkol) because of the bunch that the Israelites found there, showing how this fruit was emblematic of the region.
H0811.emploi: The word bunch appears 9 times in the Bible, primarily to designate the grapes of the vine, a major symbol of agricultural life and blessing in Israel. It is encountered mostly in poetic context: in the Song of Solomon, where it becomes a metaphor for seduction and beauty of the body; in the prophets (Isaiah, Micah), where it alternately symbolizes divine blessing or moral degeneration. In Deuteronomy 32:32 and Isaiah 65:8, the bunch carries a moral judgment: it can be poisoned (reflecting sin) or healthy (reflecting faithfulness). Each usage plays on this dual richness: the concrete fruit and its symbolic weight.
H0811.portee: The bunch reminds us that God has promised a fertile and generous land to His people. It invites us to recognize the concrete signs of His blessing in creation. But it also warns that this fertility can be turned towards evil: a noble vine can produce poison if it becomes perverted, an image of what happens when a heart receives God's gifts without remaining faithful to Him.

sens: Amorite living in Hebron, brother of Mamre and Aner
Fertile valley near Hebron, famous for its vineyards
H0812G.detail:
1. Eshcol is an Amorite chief who lived in Hebron during the time of the patriarch Abraham. He was the brother of Mamre and Aner, three men who formed an alliance with Abraham to help him in his battles (Genesis 14:13). He appears alongside his brothers when Abraham must rescue his nephew Lot captured by enemy kings, and all three share the spoils of this victory (Genesis 14:24). He is a trusted companion of the patriarch in the Promised Land.
2. The name Eshcol also designates a region, the valley of Eshcol near Hebron, which became famous for the exceptional quality of its grapes and abundant vineyards. It is a place of fertility and prosperity in the lands that Abraham occupied.
H0812G.origine: The Hebrew name Eshcol literally means "bunch" or "cluster" — an image that evokes the richness of the harvest and abundance. This same word is found in Hebrew to designate a bunch of grapes, which explains why the valley bears this name: it was such a fertile region that it was famous for its magnificent bunches of grapes. The name connects the character to the generous land that God promised to Abraham and his descendants.
H0812G.emploi: Eshcol appears twice in the Bible, always in Genesis 14, where he plays a minor but significant role. He is one of the three Amorite brothers (along with Mamre and Aner) who form an alliance with Abraham. They first appear when Abraham learns of Lot's abduction (Genesis 14:13), and then again when Abraham distributes the spoils of his victory: Eshcol and his brothers receive their share, thus acknowledging their faithfulness in the battle alongside the patriarch (Genesis 14:24). These brief mentions show how local men, the Amorites, bond with Abraham and support him in his adventures in the Promised Land.
H0812G.portee: Eshcol illustrates a reality often forgotten: Abraham did not live alone in Canaan, but among local populations with whom he formed bonds of friendship and alliance. The very name, "bunch" or "abundance," reminds us that the Promised Land was not empty, but fertile and generous, capable of nourishing those who lived there. These three Amorite brothers show that God's providence provided Abraham with human allies, neighbors he could count on.

sens: Fertile valley near Hebron, in Canaan
Region renowned for its vineyards and abundant fruits
H0812H.detail: 1. Eshcol is a valley located in the region of Canaan, near Hebron. It is there that the twelve spies sent by Moses discovered a bunch of grapes so enormous that it took two men to carry it (Numbers 13:23). 2. The name means "bunch" in Hebrew, and the valley bears this name precisely because the Israelites found this remarkable bunch of grapes there, as well as other fruits like pomegranates and figs, testifying to the exceptional fertility of the promised land (Numbers 13:24).
H0812H.origine: The Hebrew name Eshcol comes from the word meaning "bunch" (of grapes). The valley received this memorable name after the spies cut the famous bunch that symbolized the abundance and fertility of the promised land. It is a typical example in the Bible where a place derives its name from a significant event that took place there.
H0812H.emploi: Eshcol appears only four times in the Bible, all in the account of the exploration of Canaan by the twelve spies (Numbers 13:23-24 and Deuteronomy 1:24), as well as in the reminder of this event in Numbers 32:9. This valley holds crucial importance: it is the place where the Israelites had tangible proof of the richness of the land that God promised them. The account emphasizes that it is precisely in this region that the spies discovered the exceptional fruits meant to encourage them to conquer the territory.
H0812H.portee: Eshcol reminds the reader that God never promises His blessings without concrete evidence. The bunch of grapes that could only be carried by two symbolizes divine abundance: too rich for one man. This account invites the believer to recognize the signs and earnest that God gives of His promises, despite the obstacles that stand in the way.

sens: son of Gomer, grandson of Japheth
people from the north of Asia Minor
H0813G.detail: 1. Ashkenaz is a man from the genealogy of Noah, son of Gomer and grandson of Japheth. He appears in the genealogical lists at the beginning of Genesis (Genesis 10:3) as the founder of a family branch, alongside his brothers Riphat and Togarmah.
H0813G.origine: The name Ashkenaz literally means "man like scorched fire scattered," an image perhaps evoking a natural disaster or dispersion. He is a figure from patriarchal times, placing this character in the earliest period of human history after the flood.
H0813G.emploi: Ashkenaz is mentioned twice in the Bible, once in Genesis 10:3 and once in the parallel list of 1 Chronicles 1:6. These two occurrences are genealogical enumerations: they situate Ashkenaz in the lineage of Japheth, one of Noah's three sons. Over time, Ashkenaz came to designate a people from the north, likely established in Asia Minor or around Bithynia, far to the east and north of the peoples known from the biblical Middle East.

sens: Northern kingdom mentioned in the Bible
H0813H.detail: Aschkenaz is a people or a northern kingdom, called alongside other powers to fight against Babylon. The prophet Jeremiah invokes it in a vision where God mobilizes the nations against the city of Nebuchadnezzar: "Prepare the nations against her, call against her the kingdoms of Ararat, Minni, and Aschkenaz" (Jeremiah 51:27). It is a name that symbolizes a military force from the north, associated with the destruction of Babylon.
H0813H.origine: Aschkenaz is the name of a descendant of Japheth in the genealogy of Genesis (Genesis 10:3). The name likely refers to a people or territory in the northern Middle East, perhaps in Bithynia or Armenia. Its use in Jeremiah 51 makes this historical name a prophetic call to a distant warrior power.
H0813H.emploi: Aschkenaz appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Jeremiah 51:27. The context is prophetic: God commands the northern nations—Ararat, Minni, and Aschkenaz—to rise up and destroy Babylon. This passage dates from the time of exile, and the name evokes a formidable northern power, likely a nation from the Caucasus or Asia Minor. Its use is solely geopolitical and military.
H0813H.portee: This verse reveals that God controls empires and peoples, even distant ones, to execute His judgment. Although Babylon was then the greatest power in the world, God uses it as an instrument of discipline against His people, and then calls others to break it. It is a promise that no empire lasts forever against the divine will.

sens: Gift offered out of respect or submission, especially from one king or power to another
Precious goods brought as tribute or valuable merchandise
H0814.detail:
1. A present is a gift offered, particularly a ceremonial gift between great figures or between a subject and a king. In Psalm 72, distant kings—those from Tarshish, Sheba, and Saba—offer presents to the king of Israel: it is a recognition of his greatness and authority. The gesture shows submission or respect.

2. This present can be a precious commodity, a valuable item exchanged. In Ezekiel 27, ivory and ebony horns are mentioned as presents: these are rare and costly goods that the people of Dedan bring to the port of Tyre, the great commercial market of the ancient East.
H0814.origine: The Hebrew word אֶשְׁכָּר comes from a root that evokes the idea of "reward" or "wage," related to exchange and transaction. It is a concrete word: it primarily designates the material good given or received in return for a service, honor, or trade. The image is that of a gift that creates a relationship: one offers a present to honor someone or to seal an agreement.
H0814.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Psalm 72, it describes the tributes and presents that distant kings bring to the ideal king of Israel, depicting universal respect and submission. In Ezekiel 27, in the lament over Tyre, it refers to the precious goods—ivory and ebony—that neighboring peoples pay and bring: it is the prosperous trade of the great merchant city. In both cases, the word paints wealth and prestige: receiving presents signifies being great and powerful.
H0814.portee: This word reminds us that in the Bible, presents are never mere trivial gifts: they express respect, recognition, or alliance. Offering a present establishes or honors a relationship. For the Christian reader, this sheds light on how the Bible views the exchange between humans and God: not as a neutral commercial transaction, but as one of honor and relationship.

sens: Shrub or small tree with hard wood, fine leaves, and small white or pink flowers, which grows in arid and salty regions
Tree planted as a memorial or place of worship
Tree serving as refuge or shelter
H0815.detail:
1. The tamarisk is a robust shrub with very fine leaves, capable of surviving in the salty and arid terrains of the ancient Near East. It is a hard and durable wood, useful for construction. Abraham plants several at Beersheba (Genesis 21:33) to mark the well and the holy place where he calls upon the Lord.
2. The tamarisk can symbolize a memorial or a sanctuary. Planted by Abraham, it becomes a place of prayer and personal worship, a landmark in the desert where the presence of God is invoked.
3. This tree also offers shade and protection. Saul sits under the tamarisk at Gibeah (1 Samuel 22:6), and the remains of Saul are buried under the tamarisk at Jabesh (1 Samuel 31:13), suggesting a place considered worthy or sacred to honor the dead.
H0815.origine: The Hebrew word אֵשֶׁל (ashel) designates this particular tree of the Levant. Its exact etymology remains debated, but the tamarisk was well known throughout the ancient Near East for its qualities of adaptation to desert and saline environments. The name applies to a very specific tree, recognizable by its distinctive botanical properties.
H0815.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. Abraham plants tamarisks at Beersheba as an act of establishing personal worship (Genesis 21:33). In 1 Samuel, the tamarisk becomes a landmark: Saul sits there to hold his royal court at Gibeah (22:6), and Saul's bones receive an honorable burial under the tamarisk at Jabesh (31:13). These three uses show that the tamarisk was regarded as a notable tree, worthy of marking important places or decisive moments.
H0815.portee: The tamarisk reminds us that even in the aridity of the desert, God provides life and offers places of refuge. When Abraham plants this tree and calls upon the Lord there, he establishes a memorial of faith in an inhospitable territory. For the believer, this tree symbolizes how God blesses the places where we invoke Him and transforms barren spaces into areas of encounter with Him.

sens: To commit an offense, a transgression against the law or against someone
To be recognized, judged guilty of an infraction
To incur a condemnation, to suffer a punishment for one's guilt
To become sorrowful, ruined as a result of an offense
H0816.detail:
1. To commit an offense, a transgression: this means doing something wrong, either deliberately or through negligence. Leviticus 5:4 describes someone who swears lightly and, upon realizing later their commitment, becomes guilty of violating that oath. It is the act of sinning, of acting wrongly against a commandment or a person.
2. To be recognized as guilty, to be judged as such: this means being declared responsible for one's fault. Numbers 5:6 speaks of a person who becomes guilty by committing unfaithfulness to the Lord — that is, who is identified as having transgressed. It is the verdict that weighs on the transgressor.
3. To suffer punishment or condemnation for one's guilt: this is the consequence of the fault. Psalms 34:22 says that "evil kills the wicked, and the enemies of the righteous are punished" — meaning that the guilty one bears the weight of their sin. Hosea 5:15 shows the people who must confess their guilt to find forgiveness.
4. To become sorrowful or ruined: one nuance of the word designates the state of one who has caused harm, who has committed an infraction and suffers the personal ravages of it. It conveys the idea that sin leaves a mark of destruction on the one who commits it.
H0816.origine: The Hebrew verb אָשַׁם (asham) is related to a root that evokes the idea of guilt and desolation. It denotes the transition from innocence to a state of guilt, and sometimes the ruin or devastation that follows. The word is primarily used in the legal texts of the Pentateuch, where it qualifies one who transgresses the commandments. A derived noun, אָשָׁם (asham), designates the sin offering or guilt offering — this sacrifice that was offered to atone for the fault and restore the relationship with God.
H0816.emploi: The verb appears 32 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in Leviticus (where it designates one who transgresses a commandment, whether voluntarily or not, and must present an offering), in the Psalms, and in the Prophets (where it characterizes one who has sinned and must acknowledge their guilt or suffer the consequences). In Leviticus 4:13, the entire assembly becomes guilty by transgressing unintentionally; in Leviticus 5, specific cases of guilt are enumerated. In the Prophets, particularly Hosea and Jeremiah, the people of Israel are declared guilty of forsaking the Lord. The word thus designates both the act of sinning, the fact of being held responsible, and sometimes the punishment that results from it.
H0816.portee: This word reminds the believer that sin is not an abstraction: it is a real guilt, a transgression that creates a rupture with God and has concrete consequences. It also invites one to acknowledge their guilt before God, as Hosea teaches — this acknowledgment is the path to forgiveness and restoration. In Christ, the believer sees their guilt removed by the sacrifice that satisfies God's justice.

sens: The state of one who has committed an offense, a transgression against God or against others
The fault, the offense, the trespass committed
What follows: the responsibility to repair or compensate for the harm done
The sacrifice or offering brought to atone for this guilt
H0817.detail: 1. Guilt is primarily the state of one who has become guilty: it is the weight of a transgression, the feeling or reality of having committed an offense. Abimelech tells Abraham that by taking his wife, he would have made him "guilty," meaning he would have placed him in a state of guilt before God (Genesis 26:10). It is this moral burden that the word designates. 2. The word also designates the offense itself, the wrong committed. When Leviticus speaks of a man who "has become guilty before the Lord," it is the act of transgression that is in view, this rupture of the covenant with God (Leviticus 5:19). 3. Guilt creates an obligation to repair: in Numbers 5:7, one who has committed a fault must restore "in full the object wrongfully acquired" and add a fifth, which is the due repair. 4. The guilt offering (in Hebrew asham) is the special offering prescribed to atone for this guilt: a ram or lamb offered to the Lord according to the prescriptions of Leviticus 5 to 7, to restore the broken relationship between the sinner and God.
H0817.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning fundamentally "to be guilty" or "to be enslaved." It expresses the idea of a debt or obligation that weighs on one who has transgressed. In the Law, this word has specialized to designate the guilt offering, one of the major sacrifices of Israelite worship. The same root is found in verbal and adjectival forms designating the state of guilt.
H0817.emploi: The word occurs 41 times, primarily in Leviticus, which regulates its modalities; it is also found in Numbers and in 1 Samuel regarding the ark. In Leviticus (chapters 5 to 7 and 14), asham designates the guilt offering: a specific rite, offered notably for hidden faults, thefts, or offenses against the sanctuary. In 1 Samuel 6, the Philistines bring to the Lord a guilt offering by returning the ark. The word is also used broadly for guilt itself: the state of the guilty (Genesis 26:10) or the wrongful act (Numbers 5:7). In Isaiah 53:10, the suffering servant becomes a guilt offering for humanity, which announces the redemptive significance of the sacrifice.
H0817.portee: This word reminds the believer of a central truth: guilt is real and creates a debt, but it can be removed by a sacrifice brought to God. For Israel, the guilt offering provided concrete repair and a path to reconciliation. For the Christian, Isaiah 53:10 points to Jesus as the definitive guilt offering, the one whose sacrifice ends the guilt of all who believe. This illuminates the profound meaning of Christ's death: it repairs what we have broken.

sens: Who has committed a fault, a crime, or a sin
Who incurs an obligation to atone for their guilt through a sacrifice
H0818.detail:
1. A guilty person is one who has violated a law or committed a reprehensible act for which they bear responsibility. Joseph's brothers acknowledge being "guilty" toward him for having sold him in the past: they knew it was wrong, and they feel the guilt years later (Genesis 42:21). Similarly, King David is declared "guilty" for not recalling his exiled son, as if he had transgressed a moral standard (2 Samuel 14:13).
2. In the Hebrew religious context, being guilty also means being required to offer a specific atoning sacrifice: the guilt offering or sacrifice for sin. Men who have married foreign women in violation of the Law commit to "offer" a ram as a guilt offering, an act that expresses both their acknowledgment of sin and their desire for atonement before God (Ezra 10:19).
H0818.origine: The Hebrew word אָשֵׁם comes from a primitive root that evokes the idea of guilt and the legal obligation that follows. In biblical Hebrew, this word carries the image of a person marked by fault, obliged to justify themselves or repair the consequences. The noun אָשָׁם (the guilt offering) derives from the same root and shows how the concept of guilt was inseparable, in Israel's sacrificial system, from the obligation to present a reparative offering.
H0818.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, each time in a serious situation. It first describes moral consciousness: Joseph's brothers express their long-standing guilt when misfortune catches up with them. It is also used in a political and ethical sense: an authority can be "guilty" of not acting justly (2 Samuel 14:13). Finally, it takes on its full meaning in sacrificial vocabulary: one who is guilty before God must honor this guilt through the prescribed sacrifice, making it a central word in the theology of atonement in Israel.
H0818.portee: This word reminds us that guilt is not just a fleeting feeling: it engages moral responsibility before God and others. For the believer, it shows that acknowledging one's guilt — as Joseph's brothers did — is the first step toward atonement and forgiveness. The guilt offering mentioned here foreshadows the atoning work of Christ, who alone can permanently remove the guilt of the believer.

sens: State of one who has committed a fault, a transgression
Faulty act, sin, violation of a law or order
Responsibility for causing harm, offense
Feeling or declaration of being guilty before God
H0819.detail:
1. Guilt is the state of a person who has sinned or committed a fault. It is not a mere impression, but a reality: one who has transgressed God's law truly bears the weight of their fault. In Leviticus 4:3, the priest who has sinned renders the entire people "guilty" — his transgression has collective consequences.
2. The word also designates the faulty act itself, the sin concretely committed. It is the action that creates guilt. The fault can be great or small: in Leviticus 5:26, someone is forgiven for "the fault they have committed."
3. Guilt can also signify the harm caused, the offense against God or others. In 2 Chronicles 28:10, the people ask their prisoners: "Are you not guilty before the Lord?" — their guilt is a debt, a violation of the covenant with God.
4. Sometimes the word emphasizes the aspect of personal responsibility, the fact of being liable and subject to punishment. In Ezra 9:7, the people confess that they have "been greatly guilty" since past generations, bearing the burden of their iniquities.
H0819.origine: The Hebrew word ashma comes from a root that expresses the idea of "guilt" or "fault." It is related to words designating the "ram" (used for atoning sacrifices) and the general idea of transgression. In biblical Hebrew, guilt is not a psychological abstraction, but an objective reality: one who has sinned incurs a sort of debt to God that must be erased through confession, forgiveness, or an atoning offering.
H0819.emploi: This word appears 17 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the legal books (Leviticus) and in later historical narratives (Chronicles, Ezra). It carries several nuances depending on the context. In Leviticus, guilt arises from specific transgressions (sins of ignorance, ritual faults) and is atoned for through sacrifices. In Chronicles and Ezra, especially during moments of national crisis (exile, restoration), the word takes on a collective dimension: all Israel is "guilty" due to the unfaithfulness of kings or ancestors (2 Chronicles 33:23; Ezra 9:7). The word can also describe the act that renders one guilty ("to sin" Israel in 1 Chronicles 21:3) or the responsibility before God (2 Chronicles 28:10).
H0819.portee: This word reminds the reader that sin is not an illusion or a matter of opinion: it creates real guilt before God. But it also shows that Israel was never trapped in its guilt — Leviticus offered ways of purification and atonement. For the Christian, this word sheds light on why Jesus had to bear our guilt: we are truly responsible for our actions, but grace can set us free from it.

sens: state of wealth or resources in great quantity
figuratively: material or spiritual prosperity that should satisfy, but does not appease the one who enjoys it
H0820.detail:
1. The word denotes abundance, a profusion of goods or resources — what is present in large numbers, in excessive quantity. In Isaiah 59:10, the prophet speaks of the people saying that "in the midst of abundance we resemble the dead": even surrounded by riches and material goods, Israel feels empty and powerless, as if spiritually dead.
2. Figuratively, abundance represents everything that should suffice for satisfaction, but cannot fill the heart thirsty for a true relationship with God. It is the image of external prosperity that hides an inner poverty: one has everything materially, but remains lost, unable to find the way.
H0820.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes strength, fullness, amplitude. Its suggestive use in Isaiah highlights the contrast between the visual wealth of the world and spiritual blindness: it is because one has much that one forgets that one can lack the essential. The Bible uses this word to show that true life is not found in the multiplication of goods.
H0820.emploi: The word appears only once in the Segond, in Isaiah 59:10. The prophet uses it in a poignant picture of God's judgment on Israel: the people have an abundance of goods, but they stumble like the blind, they do not see, they are spiritually dead. It is in this context of moral condemnation that the word takes on its force: abundance saves no one if the heart has turned away from God.
H0820.portee: This word reminds the Christian of a humbling truth: material wealth is never a sign of God's spiritual blessing, and it can even become a prison. It invites one to ask: am I rich in God, or only in possessions? External abundance without the presence of God is nothing but death.

sens: Division of the night into time segments for surveillance or guarding
Period of time during which a sentinel or guard keeps watch
Specific moment of the night, particularly the hours before dawn
State of vigilance and personal meditation during the night hours
H0821.detail:
1. The watch is a division of the night established to organize guard shifts. The Israelites divided the night into several watches, as shown in Judges 7:19: Gideon attacks at the "beginning of the middle watch," meaning at a determined hour of the night according to this system of division.
2. It is also the period during which someone stands guard or watches. At the morning watch, the Lord looked at the Egyptian camp (Exodus 14:24): this is the hour when the sentinels were vigilant.
3. The watch refers to a specific moment of the night, particularly just before dawn. Saul strikes the Ammonites "at the morning watch" (1 Samuel 11:11), a moment when the night is coming to an end.
4. The word takes on a personal and spiritual meaning: the watches of the night are the hours when the psalmist prays and meditates. In Psalm 119:148, the one who worships the Lord "anticipates the watches" by rising before the usual hour to pray, demonstrating a voluntary dedication.
H0821.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to keep" or "to observe." It is related to the concrete practice of night watch: dividing the night into portions so that each person takes turns watching over the camp or place. This practice was common in the ancient world, particularly in Egypt and Israel. The word evokes both the action of keeping watch (staying awake) and the resulting time segment.
H0821.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the Old Testament. Four occurrences refer to the morning or midnight watches during decisive military events: Exodus 14:24, Judges 7:19, and 1 Samuel 11:11 show that the Lord intervenes at specific moments, often at the change of guard. Three uses in the Psalms (63:7, 90:4, 119:148) and Lamentations 2:19 reveal a more spiritual usage: the watches become the time when the believer turns to God in prayer and meditation. The context thus shifts from military (watching for an enemy) to personal (dialogue with God).
H0821.portee: This watch teaches the believer that God acts in history at critical hours, often when the guardians of the natural world are tired or distracted. It also invites a personal practice of night prayer, not imposed by a military role, but arising from a heart that seeks God before the day breaks. The spiritual watches of the psalmist illustrate a voluntary dedication that honors God.

sens: openwork grille that closes or adorns a window
curious or discreet glance thrown through an opening
H0822.detail:
1. The lattice is an assembly of crossed bars that form an openwork pattern. At the window, it allows light and air to pass while partially obscuring the view from the inside to the outside. It is a kind of screen or blind that preserves privacy. Sisera's mother looks "through the lattice" of her window (Judges 5:28), suggesting that she observes the outside without being clearly seen herself.
2. By extension, the word refers to the action of looking discreetly or with restraint through such an opening. It is a filtered, partial, almost hidden glance. In Proverbs 7:6, the narrator says he "looked through [his] lattice," evoking the position of one who observes without revealing themselves, spying rather than conversing openly.
H0822.origine: The Hebrew word אֶשְׁנָב (eshnavh) is probably related to the root שׁנב (shnavh), which evokes the idea of "looking furtively" or "leaning in." The lattice is thus named after the characteristic action performed with it: looking through. The same root appears in other words related to oblique or furtive vision. It is a very concrete image: the object is defined by the use made of it.
H0822.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, always in the singular and in the context of a window. In Judges 5:28, Sisera's mother spies through the lattice of her window, waiting for her son to return from battle (he will not return). In Proverbs 7:6, the poet positions himself at his window with his lattice to observe a scene of seduction. In both cases, the lattice marks the boundary between two worlds: the protected interior and the observed outside, and it underscores the attitude of the one who looks—a glance that remains hidden, discreet, often laden with expectation or curiosity.
H0822.portee: The lattice reminds us that human vision is always partial and filtered. Sisera's mother sees only what the lattice allows her to see; she is unaware of the future. For the believer, this evokes the importance of humble trust in the face of what we cannot see or fully understand. The lattice is also an image of intimacy and home: it is from one's own protected space that one observes the world.

sens: City of Judah located in the coastal plain
H0823.detail: Ashnah is a small city in the territory of the tribe of Judah, mentioned twice in the list of cities that Joshua enumerates during the division of the promised land (Joshua 15:33 and 15:43). It was located in the plain region, a fertile area between the mountain of Judah and the Mediterranean coast.
H0823.origine: The name Ashnah literally means "I will change" or "change," formed from a Hebrew root denoting transformation or modification. This type of place name may evoke an event or characteristic of the location at the time it received this name.
H0823.emploi: Ashnah appears only in the book of Joshua, in chapter 15, which systematically lists the cities assigned to Judah during the conquest of Canaan. It is mentioned twice in this enumeration (verses 33 and 43), indicating that it was an identified and well-known locality in the eyes of those compiling these lists. Its presence in this official register confirms its importance in the Judean territory, although its later history is not reported elsewhere in the Scriptures.

sens: City of the tribe of Judah
H0824.detail: Eshean is a small city located in Judea, in the territory allocated to the tribe of Judah. It appears in the list of cities that Joshua assigns to Judah after the conquest of Canaan (Joshua 15:52).
H0824.origine: The name means "support" in Hebrew, probably referring to a geographical feature or the function of this locality. Its etymology relates to the idea of support or a point of reference.
H0824.emploi: Eshean appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 15:52, in the enumeration of cities assigned to the tribe of Judah. It is mentioned alongside Arab and Duma, among the localities in southern Judea. Its precise geographical identification today remains uncertain, but it was one of the many settlements that constituted the urban and administrative network of the territory of Judah.

sens: A person who claims to read the future or understand secrets in the stars and celestial phenomena
A magician or diviner who practices occult arts and esoteric formulas
H0825.detail:
1. An astrologer is someone who claims to derive hidden knowledge or predict the future by observing the stars, planets, and celestial phenomena. It is a supposedly superior knowledge, but it relies on magic rather than true wisdom. In Babylon, these men advised the king and played an important political role: Daniel 1:20 shows that the astrologers of the Babylonian king were questioned on matters requiring wisdom and intelligence, like the other magicians of the kingdom.
2. More broadly, this word designates any practitioner of esoteric and occult arts: enchanters, diviners, spirit invokers. In Daniel 2:2, the king calls together "the magicians, the astrologers, the enchanters, and the Chaldeans" — a list of specialists in the invisible world and supernatural powers according to pagan beliefs. The astrologer shared this role with others who claimed to access forbidden mysteries.
H0825.origine: The Hebrew word אַשָּׁף (ashshaph) comes from a root meaning "to charm," "to enchant." It literally designates one who practices enchantment and witchcraft. The Aramaic אָשַׁף (ashshaph) is identical and confirms that this term is used in the Babylonian context of the Book of Daniel. The word evokes the idea of one who "binds" through magical words, seeking to control invisible forces.
H0825.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in the Book of Daniel in Aramaic context (Daniel 1:20 and 2:2). In these two passages, it is part of a series of titles designating the occult advisors of Nebuchadnezzar II, king of Babylon. In Daniel 1:20, the astrologers are presented as rivals in wisdom — a contrast emphasized by the fact that Daniel and his three companions surpass them "ten times." In Daniel 2:2, they are summoned by the king as supposed resources to solve a mystery (the forgotten dream): it is a desperate appeal to magic in the face of the impossible. These two uses show the astrologer in his role as a reputed Babylonian sage, but always defeated by the true wisdom that God gives.
H0825.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that claiming to know hidden secrets, reading the future in the stars, or commanding invisible powers is the opposite of true wisdom. The Bible values trust in God alone and rejects occult arts. Moreover, it shows that those who seek this false wisdom are left without answers (the king cannot see his dream), while God reveals his mysteries to those who seek him (Daniel receives the vision). It is an invitation to renounce superstitions and seek the truth from God.

sens: One who claims to read the future or secrets in the stars and celestial phenomena
Practitioner of occult arts and magic, advisor to the king in ancient empires
H0826.detail:
1. An astrologer is a man who claims to know the future or hidden truths by observing the stars, the positions of the planets, and celestial phenomena. In Daniel 2:27, the astrologers are mentioned alongside the wise men and diviners as unable to reveal the secret that the king requests: the word designates those who supposedly master the secrets of the heavens.
2. More broadly, it is a practitioner of magical and occult arts, an advisor to the king in Eastern courts — like Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar. In Daniel 5:11, we see that the king establishes these astrologers as leaders among the scholars of the kingdom, entrusting them with positions of authority. They appear in the list of royal experts, alongside magicians and diviners, without the Bible valuing them.
H0826.origine: This Aramaic word (אָשַׁף) comes from the same Hebrew root (אַשָּׁף, used in Hebrew) and initially designates one who conjures, who utters words of magical power. The root evokes the idea of enchanting, casting a spell, or manipulating invisible forces through words and secret knowledge. The term is used in a pagan context to describe the practices of the wise men of Babylon.
H0826.emploi: This word appears only in Aramaic in the New Testament (six occurrences in Daniel, chapters 2, 4, and 5). It regularly returns in the accounts of the crises of King Nebuchadnezzar: when he asks his wise men to interpret a dream or a mysterious inscription, the astrologers are always mentioned among those who fail to respond. They form an official class of royal advisors, but the Bible emphasizes that their knowledge is incapable of uncovering true secrets — it is Daniel, by the Spirit of the living God, who alone can do so. The word paints a picture of false human wisdom in the face of true divine revelation.
H0826.portee: This word reminds us that all supposed occult sciences — whether they adorn themselves with magic, astrology, or divination — are vain before the God who holds history and reveals secrets to his prophets. The astrologers fail where Daniel succeeds: it is a call to place our trust not in hidden arts or human knowledge, but in the revelation of God.

sens: Portable case for carrying an archer's arrows
Set of arrows themselves
Place where God stores his instruments of judgment or his servants
H0827.detail:
1. A quiver is primarily the case that an archer carries with him to keep his arrows and have them ready at hand in battle. It is a concrete object of the ancient warrior, as seen when Elam "bears the quiver" in Isaiah 22:6.
2. The word then designates the arrows themselves contained in the quiver, as when the psalmist speaks of "filling his quiver" with children (Psalms 127:5), who are compared to the warrior's arrows.
3. The quiver becomes a spiritual image: God hides his servants or instruments in his quiver (Isaiah 49:2), or fills his quiver with the arrows of judgment that he launches against enemies (Jeremiah 5:16, Lamentations 3:13). The quiver thus becomes a symbol of divine power, the secret place from which God's strikes emerge.
H0827.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes the idea of gathering, collecting. The quiver is therefore literally what "gathers" or "collects" the arrows. It is a specifically Hebrew word, concrete and warrior-like, rooted in the experience of ancient Near Eastern battles.
H0827.emploi: This word appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, always with the same image: the quiver of the warrior or the armed people (Job, Isaiah 22, Jeremiah). But the Bible uses it mostly figuratively: the quiver becomes a symbol of fertility (children are the arrows of the father, Psalms 127), then the image of God's hand that launches his strikes or hides his servants. In Isaiah 49:2, the prophet says that God has hidden him in his quiver like an arrow ready to be launched. In Lamentations 3:13, God's quiver is filled with arrows that pierce the body of the suffering one. The word thus glides from the military domain to the spiritual domain.
H0827.portee: This word reminds the believer that God masters all weapons and instruments of his plan. It also invites the father of a family to see his children, not as a burden, but as arrows in hand: a divine blessing and a strength. For the one who suffers, the image of God's quiver may seem terrifying; but it affirms that even the strikes appear mysteriously ordered by a hand that knows what it is doing.

sens: Chief eunuch of the Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar
Officer responsible for the training of young Israelite captives
H0828.detail: Aschpenaz is the chief of the eunuchs of King Nebuchadnezzar II of Babylon. He is a high-ranking official at the royal court tasked with selecting and training the most promising young Israelite captives. In Daniel 1:3, the king entrusts him with the specific mission of bringing children of Israel from royal blood or noble families to educate and prepare them for service in the royal palace. His role illustrates how the Babylonian administration integrated talented captives into its system, while reminding us that these young men (including Daniel) remained under foreign authority.
H0828.origine: The name Aschpenaz appears only in Daniel 1:3. Although its exact meaning is debated by scholars, the biblical narrative presents him as a high-ranking Babylonian official. His name is of Persian or Babylonian origin, which is fitting for a court officer in Babylon in the 6th century B.C. He embodies the administrative structure of the Neo-Babylonian Empire and its system of selective captivity.
H0828.emploi: Aschpenaz is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Daniel 1:3. He appears at the beginning of the account of Daniel in Babylon, as a key figure who receives the royal order to gather the young captives. Although few details are given about him, his role shows how the Babylonians captured and utilized the Israelite elite. Daniel 1 then recounts how Daniel and his three companions, presumably among the young presented to Aschpenaz, request not to eat the royal meat and remain faithful to the law of Moses.

sens: portion of meat distributed to someone
gift or gratuity
H0829.detail:
1. Portion of meat: a piece or share of meat given to eat. In context, David distributes portions of food to the people during a religious celebration, each receiving "a loaf of bread, a portion of meat, and a cake of raisins" (2 Samuel 6:19). It is a measured meat, assigned individually, not food served in bulk.
2. Gift or gratuity: the word also refers to a share given as a mark of goodwill or community sharing. The meaning extends beyond mere food: it is an act of generosity from the king towards his people, a way to honor and gather them around worship.
H0829.origine: The Hebrew word אֶשְׁפָּר (eshpar) has an obscure meaning, attested only twice in the Bible. Its precise etymology is uncertain. It belongs to the lexical field of food and measured portions. The biblical context (offerings, distributions during religious festivals) suggests a connection with well-known practices of ritual meat sharing in Israelite worship.
H0829.emploi: The word appears only twice, in two parallel passages: 2 Samuel 6:19 and 1 Chronicles 16:3. Both texts describe an identical moment: David celebrates the arrival of the Ark of the Covenant in Jerusalem and distributes food to all the people. In both cases, the "portion of meat" is part of a festive and religious distribution, associated with bread and cakes of raisins. It is a public act, engaging the king in a relationship of goodwill towards the gathered community.
H0829.portee: This word reminds us that biblical faith never separates the sacred from the profane or the physical: celebrating God involves sharing a table. David's distribution shows how a religious leader honors the people and gathers them around God by providing for their concrete needs. It is a lesson in sacred hospitality and communion.

sens: Gate of Jerusalem leading to the Valley of Hinnom, where the city's garbage and waste were thrown
H0830G.detail: 1. It is one of the main gates of Jerusalem, mentioned during the reconstruction of the walls under Nehemiah, upon the return from exile. It gets its name from its proximity to a dump where garbage, animal carcasses, and all the refuse of the city accumulated. It opens onto the Valley of Hinnom, to the east or southeast of the city, and served as a passage for evacuating waste. When Nehemiah "inspects the ruined walls" (Nehemiah 2:13), he takes this unglamorous route to assess the state of the defenses: even a gate associated with refuse had its importance in the defense plan. It is also through this gate that solemn processions pass during the dedication of the walls (Nehemiah 12:31), showing that all access points, even the humblest, are integrated into the religious life of restored Jerusalem.
H0830G.origine: The Hebrew word אַשְׁפֹּת (ashpot) comes from the root שׁפה (shafah) or a related root suggesting the idea of throwing or dumping. The word literally designates a place where refuse is discarded, a dump. It is a concrete and descriptive name, which appears only in the specific context of Jerusalem and its gates. The simplicity of the term reflects the practical reality of ancient cities: there had to be a place to dispose of waste, and this unprestigious function was assumed by a gate bearing this nickname.
H0830G.emploi: This term appears four times in the book of Nehemiah, all occurrences relating to the same gate of Jerusalem during the restoration of the walls in the 5th century B.C. Nehemiah first mentions it during his nighttime inspection tour (Nehemiah 2:13), then during the detailed description of the repair work on the gates and sections of the walls (Nehemiah 3:13-14), where several leaders are tasked with restoring this gate specifically. Finally, it reappears during the dedication procession of the walls (Nehemiah 12:31), where the choirs march "to the right on the wall, toward the gate of the refuse." It is never just a geographical element: it symbolizes the necessity, even for a restored people, to integrate the ordinary and the daily into their reconstructed life.
H0830G.portee: This gate reminds the believer that God watches over all aspects of a community's life, including the humblest and least noble. When Nehemiah restores Jerusalem, he neglects no gate, not even the gate of refuse: it is a call to the dignity of ordinary work and the importance of every detail in the building up of God's people. For the Christian, this humble gate also symbolizes redemption: what was waste and refuse can be restored and become part of a holy city.

sens: Heap of waste and debris accumulated
Place of desolation and humiliation
Symbol of misery and extreme humiliation
H0830H.detail:
1. Manure is literally a heap of garbage, ashes, and debris that is accumulated outside the city or near dwellings. It is the lowest, most despised place. In Lamentations 4:5, it is written that nobles "embrace the manure," a stark image of reversal: those who lived in luxury are reduced to lying among the garbage.

2. Manure becomes a symbol of extreme humiliation and desolation. When someone is said to be raised "from the manure," as in 1 Samuel 2:8 and Psalms 113:7, it refers to one who was at the lowest rung of the social ladder — the poor, the forgotten — and whom God raises to give a place of honor among the great. Manure represents the state of one who has nothing, who is rejected.

3. This image of manure spiritually conveys humiliation and the loss of all prestige. It does not simply describe a material situation, but the condition of one who is crushed, without hope, delivered to shame. This is why the Bible chooses it to speak of God's grace: it literally lifts the despised from the heap of garbage.
H0830H.origine: The Hebrew word ashpot comes from a root that denotes ashes and debris. It is a concrete word that paints the image of a place where all refuse and waste accumulate: a true heap of garbage. The Bible always uses it to evoke the striking contrast between humiliation and elevation, between shame and honor.
H0830H.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always marking a dramatic contrast. In 1 Samuel 2:8 and Psalms 113:7, it is the same poetic passage: God "raises the poor from the manure" and "lifts the needy" to seat them with the great and give them "a throne of glory." It emphasizes God's power to transform the fate of the weak. In Lamentations 4:5, the context is reversed: it is the ruin of Jerusalem, and manure becomes the image of downfall — those who were dressed in purple, fed with delicacies, find themselves "embracing the manure," that is, begging at the heaps of garbage to survive.
H0830H.portee: This word speaks to us of God's grace toward the humble and the forgotten. It reminds us that our dignity does not come from our possessions or social status, but from the hand of God that can lift the lowest to the highest. It is a call to compassion toward those who are brought low and a promise: God does not leave the poor in the manure.

sens: Philistine coastal city on the Mediterranean, southwest of Jerusalem
H0831.detail: Ashkelon is a port city of the Philistines, located on the Mediterranean coast southwest of Jerusalem. It was one of the major Philistine cities, comparable to Gaza, Gath, and Ekron. It appears in the accounts of Israel's conquest (Judges 1:18), in the story of Samson who goes there after solving the riddle at his wedding (Judges 14:19), and in the lists of Philistine cities that offer gifts to the God of Israel following the plagues (1 Samuel 6:17). The prophets mention it among the nations called to divine judgment: Jeremiah announces the desolation of Ashkelon (Jeremiah 47:5) and David requests that his defeat not be proclaimed there (2 Samuel 1:20). It is a real city, with a concrete geography and history in the ancient world.
H0831.origine: The Hebrew name אַשְׁקְלוֹן (Ashkelon) historically designates an ancient coastal city, well attested in extra-biblical sources. Its etymology suggests a connection with the idea of brightness or fire ("fire of infamy"), reflecting the importance and military power of this Phoenician and Philistine fortress. The term derives from an ancient root common to the languages of the Levant. It is a geographical toponym that refers to a historical reality of the ancient Mediterranean world.
H0831.emploi: Ashkelon is mentioned about eleven times in the Hebrew Bible. It appears mainly in the historical books (Judges, 1 and 2 Samuel) where it features in the accounts of conquest and the relationships between Israel and the Philistines. It frequently reappears in the prophets (Jeremiah, Amos, Zephaniah, Zechariah) as one of the enemy cities destined for divine judgment. In 2 Samuel 1:20, David orders that his defeat not be announced to Ashkelon, for it might rejoice in it.
