In Jeremiah 47:5, the prophet paints the future desolation of Ashkelon: it becomes mute, defeated. It is always a city of the Philistines, historical enemies of Israel, mentioned alongside Gaza, Gath, and Ekron.

sens: Philistine city on the Mediterranean coast
inhabitant of Ashkelon
H0832.detail:
1. Ashkelon is an important city of the Philistines, located on the Mediterranean coast southwest of Canaan. It is one of the five major Philistine cities along with Gaza, Ashdod, Gath, and Ekron, each governed by a prince (Joshua 13:3).
2. The term also refers to the inhabitant or people of Ashkelon, as one would speak of an Egyptian or a Canaanite — it is a people among the peoples of the known world of the Bible.
H0832.origine: The Hebrew name אַשְׁקְלוֹן (Ashkelon) designates this historical coastal city. Its exact etymology is uncertain, but it refers to a specific and recognized place in antiquity. The inhabitants are called Ashkelon according to the Greek form of the name used in the Segond.
H0832.emploi: This word appears only once in the Segond 1910, in Joshua 13:3, where it designates one of the five Philistine princes who control the lands that God assigns to Israel. Ashkelon represents the Philistine power established over the territory that God has promised to His people.
H0832.portee: Ashkelon symbolizes in the account of Joshua the obstacles and enemies that occupy the promised land. It serves as a reminder that victory and possession of God's inheritance are not automatic, but require faith and obedience.

sens: To go straight, to advance, to progress on a path
To lead someone straight ahead, to guide
To make happy, to declare blessed
To pronounce a blessing, to call blessed
H0833.detail:
1. The verb first describes the physical movement of someone walking straight, advancing without deviation: it is to progress on a road or in life (Proverbs 9:6: "Walk in the way of understanding").
2. In the causative form (Piel), it means to lead someone straight, to direct them — like guiding a traveler to their destination (Isaiah 1:17: "Defend the oppressed" carries the idea of straightening them out, restoring their rights).
3. By extension, the verb means to make someone happy, fulfilled, or to declare them blessed — to ensure that their life truly progresses because it is just and blessed by God (Proverbs 3:18: "Those who hold her are happy").
4. Finally, it means to pronounce a blessing on someone, to call them blessed, to speak well of them (Genesis 30:13: Leah exclaims, "How happy I am!" and names her son Asher, which means precisely "happy").
H0833.origine: The Hebrew root evokes the image of one who walks straight, who advances without deviation. It is linked to the idea of progression and uprightness. The verb has given rise to the proper name Asher (or Aser), one of Jacob's sons, whose name means "happy" — showing how the ancient Hebrews saw in uprightness and progression a path to happiness. Hebrew naturally associates the idea of "going well" (advancing straight) with being "happy" or "blessed."
H0833.emploi: This verb appears fifteen times in the Old Testament, especially in the wisdom literature (Proverbs, Psalms) and in the prophets. In the simple form (Qal), it describes the act of walking, advancing straight (Proverbs 9:6, Proverbs 4:14). In the intensive form (Piel), it emphasizes the act of making happy, blessing, directing: people declare someone "happy" or "blessed" (Genesis 30:13, Proverbs 31:28, Job 29:11), or one "leads" someone in the right path (Isaiah 1:17 speaks of "defending" the oppressed, meaning to lift them up and direct them). The last uses (Malachi 3:12 and 3:15) show people declaring others "happy." The word always paints a blessing, a happiness that comes from following the right path.
H0833.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that true blessing does not come from chance or wealth, but from walking straight, obediently to God. To be "happy" or "blessed" is to advance according to the path that God lays out, to be led and protected by Him. When we "bless" someone, we acknowledge that God has placed them on the right path. It is a word of faith: to tell someone they are "happy" is to strengthen their confidence that God is guiding and fulfilling them.

sens: who, that (subject or complement)
that, what (complement)
where, the place where
whose, the thing or person of whom
when, at the time when
since, given that
H0834A.detail:
1. This word connects a clause to a noun or pronoun that precedes it: it designates the person or thing in question. "The waters that are below the firmament" (Genesis 1:7): "that" refers to "waters" and tells us which waters are being discussed. It is the most common way to describe someone or something.
2. It can also serve as a direct complement: "all that the king had commanded" (2 Samuel 21:14). Here, "that" designates the commanded thing, the object of the action.
3. With the preposition "in," it signifies the place: "the day when I was born" (Jeremiah 20:14) designates the moment or place in question.
4. With the preposition "of," it marks possession or origin: "the land which you are about to enter" (Deuteronomy 30:18) — it is the land that belongs to you, or of which you will take possession.
5. It can also mark the moment, the time: "the day when my mother bore me" (Jeremiah 20:14) refers to the exact day of birth.
6. Sometimes it introduces a cause or explanation: it means "given that" or "since." This is the least common nuance but present in some explanatory contexts.
H0834A.origine: This word is the cornerstone of the Hebrew language for linking clauses. Its root is deep and ancient. It has no simple equivalent in English: depending on the context and the prepositions that accompany it, it translates differently (who, that, where, whose, etc.). It is a grammatical tool word, a syntactic cement that organizes the sentence by attaching descriptions and clarifications to the word they concern. Ancient Semitic languages used this word in the same way to create subordination and clarity.
H0834A.emploi: This word appears 4,041 times in the Old Testament, making it one of the most frequent words in the Hebrew Bible. It appears from Genesis and spans all the books. Its use is extremely flexible: it can introduce a short relative clause ("the tree that bears fruit," Genesis 1:11) or a long clause explaining the circumstances of an action. In historical narration (books of Samuel, Kings, Chronicles), it serves to attach details to main facts. In the laws of Leviticus and Deuteronomy, it specifies conditions and cases. In poems (Psalms, Job), it creates a close link between the image and its meaning. It is an indispensable grammatical tool, which takes on slightly different meanings depending on whether it is translated as "who," "that," "where," or "whose," but always retains its function as a logical link.
H0834A.portee: For the Christian reader, this word is the cement of biblical revelation: it is through it that God links His promises, His commands, and His descriptions of the world. Each "who" or "that" in the Bible creates a connection between a person and what they do, between a thing and its qualities, between God and His action. Learning to read these chains of connections well allows us to see how the Bible constructs its meaning, how it links the particular to the general, the present to the past and to the promises. It is a humble learning of the very logic of the sacred text.

sens: The place in which something is located or happens
The direction towards which one is going or heading
The reason, cause, or circumstance for which something occurs
What, the thing that
The moment at which something occurs
H0834B.detail:
1. The physical place where one is or where one is going: Ruth says to Naomi, "where you go I will go, where you stay I will stay" (Ruth 1:16), expressing that she will follow her mother-in-law wherever she goes. God commands the Shunammite woman to "stay where you can" during the famine (2 Kings 8:1).
2. The reason or cause of an event: "For this is the end of all mankind" (Ecclesiastes 7:2) explains why it is better to go to a house of mourning — it is the cause or circumstance that justifies it.
3. What or who: "Who will choose what is pleasing to me" (Isaiah 56:4) refers to the thing or action that pleases God.
H0834B.origine: בַאֲשֶׁר (ba-asher) is composed of the preposition בְ (be, "in, at") and the relative pronoun אֲשֶׁר (asher, "who, that"). The pronoun asher is one of the fundamental relative pronouns in ancient Hebrew, with no direct equivalent in modern French. This composition "be + asher" creates a very flexible grammatical tool for linking ideas: the place, the cause, the moment, or simply the relationship between two facts.
H0834B.emploi: This word appears 19 times in the provided biblical usages, mainly in historical narratives (Genesis, Judges, 1 Samuel, 2 Kings) and in wisdom literature (Job, Ecclesiastes). It primarily functions as an adverb of place: "where he collapsed, there he fell" (Judges 5:27) or "God heard the voice of the child in the place where he is" (Genesis 21:17). It also expresses cause or reason: "for this is the end of all mankind" (Ecclesiastes 7:2). Finally, it can introduce a relative clause: "what is pleasing to me" (Isaiah 56:4). Its meaning nuances according to the context: sometimes precisely locating, sometimes explaining a reason, sometimes linking two propositions in a more abstract manner.
H0834B.portee: For the reader of the Psalm or biblical narratives, this word shows how the Bible speaks of the world with a certain fluidity: a place is never neutral, an action always has its reasons, and obedience often consists of going where God leads. Ruth embracing Naomi's fate "where you go" invites reflection on faithfulness and total commitment. The word also reveals God's attentive providence, who sees and hears not only our words but the exact place where we are.

sens: The starting point of an action or thing: where something comes from
The place from which one comes or about which one speaks
The reason, the cause: because, since
What comes from, what results from: what one derives
H0834C.detail:
1. This word primarily expresses the origin of a thing or a good: in Genesis 31:1, Jacob accumulated his wealth "from the goods" of his father, meaning from what belonged to Laban. This is the material starting point.
2. It also designates a place or situation from which one looks or departs. When one says "from where" something comes, one indicates the geographical or circumstantial source.
3. It marks the cause or motive: "because," "since." Thus in 1 Chronicles 17:13, the Lord says he will not withdraw his grace "as I withdrew it from the one who preceded you" — there is a comparison of reason.
4. It also means what comes from something, what one derives or receives from it. In Exodus 29:27, the breast and shoulder of the ram are "what will have served for the consecration," meaning they come directly from it.
H0834C.origine: The Hebrew word is a preposition ("from") combined with the relative pronoun ("who, that, what"). This fusion creates a very common expression in Hebrew to express emanation, provenance. The preposition "from" is one of the most fundamental in the language, and it is enriched here with the relative sense: it is "because of what" or "from the moment that." This logic is found throughout the Old Testament.
H0834C.emploi: This word appears 16 times in the provided passages, mainly in Genesis, Exodus, and the historical books. It expresses either the origin of a possession (Genesis 31:1: the wealth comes from the goods of the father), or a comparison of quantity (Judges 16:30: Samson killed more at his death than he had killed in his lifetime), or a cause or reason (1 Chronicles 17:13). Its usage is very versatile: it is a small linking word that constructs nuanced, comparative, or causal thoughts. The translation varies according to the context ("who," "good," "those"), as Hebrew compresses several ideas into a single expression.
H0834C.portee: This word helps us understand how the Bible speaks of the origin of things and the reasons for our actions. By showing that everything comes from a source — whether it be God, an inheritance, or a circumstance — it invites us to reflect on the provenance of what we have and the causality of our choices. For a believer, it is a reminder that nothing appears by chance: everything has a source, and that source must be regarded with respect.

sens: in accordance with, in agreement with
at the moment when, when
because, since
in the same way as
to the extent that
according to what
H0834D.detail:
1. This word expresses conformity, agreement: an action follows what has been ordered or planned. Genesis 7:9: the animals enter the ark "two by two, as God had commanded" — they obey the received order.
2. It marks the moment, the instant when something occurs: it can mean "when," "at the moment when." Genesis 18:5: Abraham says to his visitors, "stay a little, according to how you will pass."
3. It carries a nuance of cause or reason: "because," "since." Isaiah 52:14: "Just as he has been a source of terror for many, so his appearance was marred."
4. It establishes a comparison, a resemblance between two things: "in the same way as." Deuteronomy 3:6: Israel "devoted all the cities to destruction, as we had done to Sihon."
5. It can express proportionality or a limit: "as," "to the extent that." Exodus 8:23: God separates his plagues according to the regions.
6. It introduces a relationship between what is said and what has been previously stated: "what," "that which." 1 Kings 21:11: the people "acted as Jezebel had told them."
H0834D.origine: This word results from the fusion of two Hebrew elements: "ka" (a preposition meaning "as") and "asher" (a relative pronoun, "who," "that"). Together, they form a flexible connector that expresses both identity, conformity, and temporal relationship. It is very frequently encountered in biblical Hebrew to link phrases and ideas.
H0834D.emploi: This word appears 494 times in the Hebrew Bible: it is one of the most common words. It is found in all narrative books (Genesis, Exodus, Deuteronomy, Joshua…) and in the prophets. Its usage varies: it often links an action to the received order (Genesis 7:9: the animals enter "as God had commanded"), marks obedience to divine instructions (Exodus 40:29: the altar is arranged "as the Lord had commanded"), or establishes comparisons between events (Deuteronomy 3:6: Israel acts "as we had done"). It can also indicate the moment or context: Genesis 21:1 or Exodus 12:50 show how it links cause and consequence in the narrative.
H0834D.portee: This humble yet omnipresent word invites the reader to see order and coherence: what happens is not by chance, but the result of words that have been spoken and wills that are realized. For Israel, it emphasizes that obedience to the word of God produces concrete and orderly acts. For the Christian, it reminds us that the events of sacred history unfold according to the wisdom and word of God, and that a life of faith is realizing what has been promised and commanded.

sens: state of well-being and deep satisfaction, stable happiness
blessed character, favored by God
exclamation of congratulation addressed to someone
H0835.detail: 1. The word primarily denotes an inner state of well-being, a form of happiness or satisfaction: one who experiences stable joy because their situation is good. In Deuteronomy 33:29, Moses exclaims, "Happy are you, Israel!" upon seeing the people saved by the Lord — he celebrates their privileged state. 2. It is also and especially a happiness linked to divine blessing: happy is the one whom God favors. Psalms 32:2 places the heart of happiness in God's forgiveness: "Blessed is the man to whom the Lord does not impute iniquity." It is less a sensation than a spiritual condition: being in God's good graces, living under His protection and guidance. 3. The word is also used as an interjection, an exclamation that congratulates or blesses someone: one says "Happy" to someone seen entering a good condition — Psalms 84:6 cries, "Blessed are those who place their trust in you!" to celebrate their confidence.
H0835.origine: The Hebrew root expresses the idea of walking on the right path, advancing without obstacles. The word originally evokes one who does not stumble, who progresses unhindered — an image of the path of life where all is well. This root connects to the idea of "straight walk" and produces other terms of direction and righteousness in the Bible.
H0835.emploi: This word appears 42 times in the Old Testament, especially in Psalms and Proverbs, two books that celebrate wisdom and blessed life. It often appears at the beginning of a phrase to form "beatitudes": "Blessed is the one who..." or "Blessed are those who..." (see Psalms 1:1, 119:1, Proverbs 3:13). These formulas state the conditions of true happiness according to the Bible: the fear of God, obedience to His commandments, trust in Him, mercy towards the poor. Job 5:17 even adds: "Blessed is the man whom God chastens" — misfortune received from God can become a source of blessing because it brings one back to God. The word also marks moments when the Bible recognizes favorable situations: having sons, seeing prosperous kingdoms, having wise servants.
H0835.portee: This word teaches Christians that true happiness does not depend on external circumstances (wealth, health, success), but on the relationship with God. The Bible calls "happy" the one who fears God, seeks Him, reveres Him, and obeys Him — and it promises that this blessedness is real, not illusory. It is a call to seek God's blessing rather than the satisfactions of the world, and the assurance that this quest truly leads to happiness.

sens: Son of Jacob and Zilpah
Israelite tribe descended from Asher
Territory occupied by the tribe of Asher in Canaan
H0836.detail:
1. Asher is one of the twelve sons of Jacob. He is born from the union of Jacob with Zilpah, Leah's maid. His name means "happy" in Hebrew, as Leah exclaims upon seeing him: "I am happy! For the daughters will call me happy" (Genesis 30:13). He is one of the founding patriarchs of Israel.

2. The tribe of Asher comprises all the descendants of Asher, one of the twelve tribes of Israel. The census lists show that this tribe included several families from his sons Jimna, Ishvi, and Beriah (Numbers 26:44-47). It participates in the religious and military life of the people, such as during the land distribution or cult gatherings.

3. The territory of Asher is the region that this tribe occupies in Canaan, in the northwest, near the Mediterranean. It stretches between Sidon and Mount Carmel, with cities like Achzib and Ahlab. This fertile and mountainous territory will also be redistributed upon the return from exile (Ezekiel 48).
H0836.origine: The name "Asher" comes from Hebrew and means "happy" or "blessed." It is formed from a root expressing joy and happiness. Leah, the mother of Asher, chooses this name to express her own joy at having a son. The word expresses a blessing, as confirmed by Jacob's blessing on Asher before his death: "Let him be favored with the best of foods..." (Deuteronomy 33:24).
H0836.emploi: Asher appears 41 times in the Hebrew Bible, first at his birth in Genesis 30:13, then in Jacob's genealogies (Genesis 35:26, 46:17). He is found in the census lists of the desert (Numbers 1, 26), where his descendants are counted among the warriors of Israel. The tribe of Asher receives its territorial inheritance during the conquest of Canaan (Joshua 19:24-31), with important cities. It is also mentioned in the blessings of Moses and Jacob (Deuteronomy 33:24; Genesis 49:20). After the exile, the tribe of Asher is mentioned in Ezekiel's prophetic vision regarding the renewal of Israel (Ezekiel 48).
H0836.portee: Asher reminds the reader that God has made promises to each tribe of Israel and that each has received a share of inheritance. His name, which means "happy," evokes God's blessing on those who belong to Him. The difficulties of the tribe of Asher (mentioned less often than others) show that even those who seem less prominent in the biblical narrative have a place determined by God.

sens: Happiness, bliss, state of one who is happy
Favorable chance, happy fate
H0837.detail: 1. Happiness or bliss: it is the state of well-being and contentment of one who enjoys happiness. In Genesis 30:13, Leah exclaims, "I am happy!" in Hebrew literally "With happiness!", so filled with joy at having given birth to a son, Asher, whose name itself expresses this feeling. 2. Favorable fate, happy chance: the word can also denote the fortunate circumstances that make life pleasant and fulfilling.
H0837.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root 'asher which properly means "to be right, to go straight" or "to go well." The idea is that of a straight road, a walk without obstacles, which figures the idea of happiness: a path without pitfalls. It is the same root found in the proper name Asher, the son of Jacob, and in the beatitudes of the Hebrew Bible (the 'ashrei) which sing the happiness of the righteous.
H0837.emploi: The word 'osher appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Genesis 30:13, where Leah cries out her happiness at the birth of her son. It is a moment of intense maternal emotion: Leah, who had suffered from being less loved by Jacob than Rachel, expresses her contentment and joy. The Hebrew word captures this heartfelt cry: a raw, authentic happiness that springs from finally favorable circumstances. This uniqueness makes this word particularly vivid and moving in the context in which it appears.
H0837.portee: This word reminds us that, in the biblical vision, true happiness is not a distant abstraction, but a feeling that springs from the heart when God changes our circumstances. For Leah, it is the redemption of suffering: she who was despised finds her dignity in giving a son to Jacob. Biblical happiness is always linked to divine providence and the certainty that God sees and comforts those who suffer.

sens: Lower limb of the body, part that touches the ground
Trace left by the foot while walking
Movement, direction one follows
Firmness, stability in a direction or conviction
H0838A.detail:
1. The foot is the limb of the body that bears weight and allows one to stand or walk. This is the most concrete sense of the word. Job 23:11 illustrates this well: "My foot has held fast to His steps" means that Job faithfully follows God's ways, like someone whose feet do not deviate from the path laid out.
2. The foot can also refer to the mark, the trace left while walking, the imprint of passage. This evokes the idea of following someone's steps, walking the same path: in Psalms 17:5, the psalmist asks that his "steps be upheld" in God's paths.
3. Figuratively, the foot represents movement, direction, the walk itself: it is the action of advancing toward a destination. In Proverbs 14:15, the one who lacks sense rushes "on foot," meaning without thinking, without measuring their advance.
4. The foot also symbolizes stability, moral balance, and firmness in faith or conduct. Psalms 40:3 speaks of one whose foot is established: this is someone anchored, constant in their walk with God.
H0838A.origine: The Hebrew word אֲשׁוּר comes from a root that expresses movement and progression. It is related to the image of the foot as that which carries us forward, leaving a trace. The form of the word suggests the action of walking, advancing step by step. It is a simple and concrete word, rooted in the daily experience of the body in motion.
H0838A.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in Psalms and Job, where it speaks of spiritual walking. Job 23:11 uses it in the sense of faithfully following a path, that of God. The Psalms draw on several uses: either to ask for the stability of the foot in the right path (Psalms 17:5, 40:3), or to evoke a walk without God that goes astray (Psalms 73:2). Proverbs 14:15 uses it to denote thoughtless haste. The meaning thus varies from the concrete (the physical limb) to the spiritual (the direction of life one follows).
H0838A.portee: For the reader, this word invites one to see the spiritual walk as a concrete reality: following God means being "stable on one's feet," not deviating, remaining in His paths. It encourages vigilance regarding the direction one takes each day, to ensure that our steps do not stray from the Lord's way. The foot becomes the image of coherence between conviction and conduct.

sens: movement of the foot forward
walk, gait
trace, imprint
direction, path followed
H0838B.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the elementary movement of the advancing foot: each step is a unit of walking. In Job 31:7, Job asserts that "my heart has not followed my eyes" — he speaks of not deviating from his moral path, of not taking a single step toward evil.

2. By extension, it refers to the walk itself, the way of moving, the gait of a person. In Psalms 17:11, the psalmist speaks of those who "surround us in our steps": they follow his trajectory, spying on his movements.

3. The word can also evoke the trace, the imprint left by one who walks — what remains of their passage.

4. In a figurative sense, the step represents the general direction of life, the path one follows: this is why the Bible often speaks of "keeping one's steps," "directing one's steps," being "on the right path."
H0838B.origine: The Hebrew word אַשּׁוּר comes from a root that expresses the idea of "going, walking." It is a feminine noun that concretely designates the movement of the foot. The same root appears in other Hebrew words related to movement and progression. In the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, this word is rendered by the Greek στέμμα or equivalent terms also meaning "step" or "footstep."
H0838B.emploi: This word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, always in poetic contexts of wisdom or lamentation. In Job 31:7, it illustrates moral commitment: Job defends himself by saying that his steps have not strayed from justice. In Psalms 17:11, it describes the hostile action of enemies who "surround our steps," meaning they track us, spying on each of our movements. In both cases, the step figures personal commitment — what one undertakes, where one goes morally or physically.
H0838B.portee: This word reminds the reader that every step counts, that our walk — in both the concrete and figurative sense — does not go unnoticed by God. It invites moral vigilance: our movements, our choices, our life trajectory engage our integrity. It is an invitation to walk with wisdom and righteousness.

sens: Wood from coniferous or deciduous trees, hard and sought after for fine works
Material used in the manufacture of luxury or prestigious objects
H0839.detail: 1. Boxwood is a hard and dense wood, coming from a shrub or small tree. In the ancient Near East, this wood was highly valued for its quality, density, and beautiful hue, making it ideal for delicate works and precious objects. 2. In Ezekiel 27:6, boxwood is mentioned among the sumptuous materials used to build the benches (seats or oars) of a ship, alongside worked ivory and oak wood: it is a luxury reserved for royal or high-ranking merchant vessels. The text shows that boxwood was imported and valued as a prestigious commodity.
H0839.origine: The Hebrew word אֲשׁוּרִים (ashurîm) likely designates boxwood or a similar hard and precious wood. This name evokes the possible origin of the wood or its use in commercial exploitation. Boxwood was known and worked throughout the ancient Levant for its exceptional properties: durability, fine grain, and golden color. It is a wood that symbolizes refinement and wealth.
H0839.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 27:6, in the famous description of the ship of Tyre. This passage enumerates the prestigious materials that composed this merchant vessel: the oak of Bashan (light yet sturdy wood), worked ivory, and boxwood for the benches or oars. This accumulation of noble materials showcases the splendor and commercial power of Tyre at the time.
H0839.portee: This unique mention of boxwood reminds us that the wealth of Tyre was based on its maritime trade and mastery of the finest materials in the known world. For the reader, it illustrates the vanity of earthly riches and the fall of a great power: Ezekiel enumerates these treasures shortly before announcing the ruin of the city.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah during the time of the Divided Monarchy
H0840.detail: Asareel is a man belonging to the tribe of Judah, living during the time of the Divided Monarchy (the period when the kingdom of Israel was divided into two). He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:16, where he is listed as one of the sons of Jehalléleel, himself a descendant of Judah through Caleb. His brothers are Ziph, Ziphah, and Tiria.
H0840.origine: The name Asareel means "God holds" or "God supports," formed from two Hebrew elements: the divine name El (God) and a verb expressing the idea of holding or supporting. This name reflects trust in God's protection, a common characteristic of Hebrew names that express the believer's relationship with their God.
H0840.emploi: Asareel appears only once in the Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 4:16. He is included in a genealogy of the tribe of Judah, in the list of descendants of Caleb. These genealogical lists, far from being mere enumerations, root families in the history of the chosen people and attest to their belonging to the community of Israel.

sens: Son of Asaph, musician of the sanctuary during the time of the divided monarchy.
H0841.detail: 1. Aschareéla is a Levite from the tribe of Levi, son of Asaph. He is mentioned for the first time in 1 Chronicles 25:2, where King David appointed him as a musician of the sanctuary, meaning he was responsible for the music and singing in the temple. Along with his brothers Zaccur, Joseph, and Nethania, he served under the direction of his father Asaph, who prophesied according to the orders of the king.
H0841.origine: The name Aschareéla literally means "God supports" or "God holds firm." It is a variant of another name, Jesharelah, which refers to the same person in 1 Chronicles 25:14. These two forms of the name reveal the same identity: a child of Levi entrusted to the care of God.
H0841.emploi: Aschareéla appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 25:2. He is presented as one of the sons of Asaph, the famous musician and prophet of King David. The context shows that David organized the Levites into singers and musicians for the service of the temple: Aschareéla was part of this group, responsible for leading the sacred songs and contributing to public worship.

sens: Canaanite goddess of fertility and happiness, thought to be the wife of Baal
idol or statue representing this goddess
sacred poles or trees planted near an altar in honor of this goddess
H0842.detail:
1. Astarté is a Canaanite and Babylonian deity of the pagan pantheon, worshiped as the goddess of fertility, happiness, and probably love. She was considered the wife or companion of Baal, the great god of the Canaanites. Her worship led the Israelites away from the one true God.

2. The term also refers to the physical idols or statues representing this goddess — objects that wicked kings established in the temple of Jerusalem itself, like Manasseh who "put the idol of Astarté, which he had made, in the house of which the Lord had said to David and Solomon" (2 Kings 21:7). These idols were destroyed and burned by faithful kings like Asa and Josiah.

3. Astarté also refers to the sacred poles or trees that were planted next to the altars of Baal, as symbols of the worship of this goddess. Gideon was commanded by God to tear down "the pole of Astarté that was beside" the altar of Baal (Judges 6:25-26), an act that provoked the anger of the inhabitants of his city.
H0842.origine: The Hebrew name אֲשֵׁרָה (Astarté) designates a deity of the Canaanite-Phoenician world, whose worship spread to Babylon under the name of Ishtar or Astarte. It is a proper name that identifies a specific pagan religious figure, both a goddess and the material objects of her worship. The word appears mainly in the accounts of the kings of Israel and Judah, particularly when these kings fell into idolatry.
H0842.emploi: The term "Astarté" appears about 40 times in the Old Testament, almost exclusively in the historical books (Kings, Chronicles) and the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Micah). It designates both the goddess herself and the material representations of her worship — altars, idols, poles — often associated with the worship of Baal. The Segond regularly translates אֲשֵׁרָה as "Astarté." The contexts show that the worship of Astarté was a serious symptom of Israel's unfaithfulness: it was established in "high places" (Judges 3:7, 1 Kings 14:23), taught by the prophets of Baal (1 Kings 18:19), and systematically destroyed during religious reforms (2 Kings 23:6, 2 Chronicles 34:3-4). The kings who allowed her worship attracted the anger of the Lord; those who abolished it gained His approval.
H0842.portee: For the biblical reader, Astarté embodies the danger of idolatry: the abandonment of the true God for deities of fertility and pleasure. This goddess promised only material prosperity and earthly happiness, seducing the Israelites weakened by doubt. Studying the worship of Astarté shows how deep and persistent the temptation of paganism was, requiring repeated spiritual reforms. It is a call to remain faithful to the one true God and to reject anything that claims to replace His authority.

sens: Members of the tribe of Asher, one of the twelve tribes of Israel
H0843.detail: 1. The Asérites are the descendants of Asher, son of Israel and Zilpah. Asher was one of the twelve patriarchs who founded the tribes of Israel. The name "Asher" means "happy" in Hebrew, and his descendants received the same tribal name. In Judges 1:32, we see the Asérites living among the Canaanites in the territory that had been assigned to them: they did not completely expel the local populations as the other tribes did.
H0843.origine: The word "Asérites" comes from the name of Asher, one of the sons of Jacob (Israel). The name Asher derives from a Hebrew root that means "to be happy" or "to be blessed." Asher is the eighth son of Jacob, born of Zilpah, Leah's maidservant. His brothers include Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Dan, Naphtali, Issachar, Zebulun, Joseph, and Benjamin, and his sister Dinah. The suffix "-rites" (or "-ites") is the classical form used to designate members of a tribe or descendants of an ancestor.
H0843.emploi: The term "Asérites" appears only once in the Segond, in Judges 1:32, in the context of the tribes of Israel established in the Promised Land after the conquest. This verse mentions that the Asérites did not completely drive out the Canaanites from their territory, contrary to the divine mandate. This situation reflects a recurring theme in the book of Judges: the inability or refusal of certain tribes to fully accomplish the conquest. The tribe of Asher itself is mentioned several times in the Old Testament, particularly in lists of the tribes and in territorial promises, but this term specifically designates its members or direct descendants.
H0843.portee: This word reminds us that God established Israel into twelve tribes, each with its territorial inheritance and responsibility. The example of the Asérites shows how incomplete obedience to God's commands can weaken the Church and compromise its testimony. It is a lesson for Christians: failing to fully conquer the spiritual ground that God has given us can lead to a lasting compromise with sin.

sens: Man of the tribe of Manasseh
Ancestor of a family clan
H0844G.detail:
1. Asriel is a man of the tribe of Manasseh, son of Gilead, who lived during the time of Egypt and the wilderness. His name means "I will be a prince of God." He is mentioned for the first time during the census of the people of Israel after the exodus from Egypt (Numbers 26:31).
2. Asriel also becomes the name of a family, the Asrielites, who descend from him. This family receives a portion of land in Canaan during the division of territory among the tribes (Joshua 17:2), alongside other clans from Manasseh such as the descendants of Abiezer, Helek, and Shechem.
H0844G.origine: The name Asriel literally means "I will be a prince of God," formed from Hebrew roots. It first designates a particular man from the tribe of Manasseh, son of Gilead, and then becomes the name of a family lineage bearing the suffix -ite (Asrielite) to designate its descendants and the clan they form.
H0844G.emploi: Asriel appears twice in the Bible. First in Numbers 26:31, during the census conducted in the wilderness after the exodus from Egypt, where he is cited as the son of Gilead and ancestor of the clan of the Asrielites. Then in Joshua 17:2, during the distribution of lands in Canaan, where his descendants receive a share of the territory allotted to the tribe of Manasseh, confirming the importance of his lineage among the families of Manasseh.

sens: man of the tribe of Manasseh during the time of the Exodus and the wilderness
H0844H.detail: Asriel is a character mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:14. He is the son of Manasseh, one of the two tribes descended from Joseph, and his mother was a Syrian woman, a concubine of Manasseh. He is the brother of Makir, who himself became the father of Gilead and the founder of an important branch of Manasseh. Asriel appears in the genealogy of Manasseh, testifying to the family history and alliances of the people of Israel during the time of the Exodus and the wilderness.
H0844H.origine: The name Asriel means "I will be a prince of God" or "God is my prince" — a declaration of trust in divine sovereignty over life. It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the divine name (el = God). It belongs to the family of Hebrew names that express the relationship between a man and his Creator.
H0844H.emploi: Asriel appears only once in Scripture, in 1 Chronicles 7:14, in the genealogical list of the tribe of Manasseh. He is presented as the son of Manasseh and the brother of Makir. Although his mention is brief, it is part of the record of generations that shows how the tribes of Israel were formed and how families established themselves in the promised land.

sens: Descendant d'Asriel, un chef de famille de la tribu de Manassé
H0845.detail: The Asrielites are the members of the clan descended from Asriel, a man of the tribe of Manasseh living during the time of Egypt and the wilderness. Asriel had several sons including Gilead, Abiezer, Helek, Shechem, Shemida, and Hepher, each founding their own family (Numbers 26:31). This term thus designates any member of this family group.
H0845.origine: The word comes from the proper name Asriel (אַשְׂרִיאֵל), which means "God will be my prince." The suffix "-ite" (in Hebrew י-) is a classic marker to designate descendants or members of a clan. Asriel himself was the son of Gilead and the grandson of Manasseh, making this clan an important branch of the tribe of Manasseh.
H0845.emploi: This term appears only once in the Bible, during the census of the Israelites at the end of their stay in the wilderness. Moses and the priest Eleazar count each clan of each tribe, and the Asrielites are listed as one of the families of Manasseh. It is an administrative and genealogical term that establishes the order and organization of the people of Israel.

sens: Structure verticale qui enferme ou délimite un espace
Construction ou édifice en tant que structure physique
H0846.detail:
1. A wall is a vertical structure, typically made of stone or brick, that encloses a building or delineates a property. It is the side of a construction. In the two passages of Ezra where this word appears, the Persian officials ask Zerubbabel and the Jewish elders who gave them the order to build the house of the Lord and to raise its walls — that is, to reconstruct the Temple and its enclosures (Ezra 5:3, 5:9).
2. By extension, the word can refer to the building itself or its physical structure, as a building is merely an assembly of walls. Here, raising the walls of the Temple means restoring the sanctuary in its entirety.
H0846.origine: This Aramaic word is related to the Hebrew שׁוּר (shur), which also means "wall." Aramaic and Hebrew are two closely related Semitic languages spoken and written in the ancient Near East. The word likely comes from a root originally designating what "closes" or "surrounds" — the fundamental idea of delimitation and protection. In Aramaic, this form is attested specifically in official documents from the time of the reconstruction of the Temple after the exile.
H0846.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Bible, both in the same context: the two verses in the book of Ezra (5:3 and 5:9). It concerns the official correspondence between the Persian governors and the government of Jerusalem regarding the reconstruction of the Temple after the Babylonian exile (circa 515 B.C.). The Persian officials Tattenai and Shethar-Bozenai question the Jewish leaders about the authorization to raise the walls of the Temple. The word is used in a precise administrative and legal context: it designates the walled structures of the sacred Temple that the Jews were rebuilding.
H0846.portee: This humble word — a simple reference to stacked stones — inscribed in a political document, reminds us that the reconstruction of the Temple after the exile was not merely a spiritual matter: it was a concrete, visible project that required authorization and could be criticized. The walls of the Temple embodied the return of God's people to their land and the restoration of their worship; that is why the Persian authorities scrutinized them closely. The reader thus sees that God's faith is also expressed in materiality and political order.

sens: habitants de la ville d'Eshtaol
H0848.detail: 1. The Eshtaolites are the inhabitants of the city of Eshtaol, located in Judah. The term designates this group as it is associated with a specific geographical and familial origin in the genealogy of the descendants of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:53).
H0848.origine: The word comes from Eshtaol (אֶשְׁתָּאוֹל), whose original meaning was "I will be implored" or "I will be answered," evoking the idea of responding to a prayer. The inhabitants bear the name of their city and are counted among the great families of the lands of Judah.
H0848.emploi: The only biblical use of the term is found in 1 Chronicles 2:53, where it lists the descendants and families from Kiriath-jearim, a region of Judah. The Eshtaolites are mentioned alongside other family groups like the Zorathites, indicating that they formed a recognizable community in the Judean territory during the historical period covered by Chronicles.

sens: Revolt, insurrection against established authority
Act of rising up, engaging in revolt
H0849.detail:
1. The word denotes an act of open revolt, an insurrection against the existing power. In the two passages from the book of Ezra, it refers to the city of Jerusalem accused by its enemies of having "engaged in sedition" against the Persian kings (Ezra 4:15, 4:19) — a serious political act that threatens the established order.
2. It is also the general attitude of rebellion: the act of standing up, engaging in a hostile contestation of power. The repetition of the word in both verses (Ezra 4:15 and 4:19) shows that it is an old habit of Jerusalem to rise up against its masters.
H0849.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of rising up, standing up, hence the image of the body rising in opposition. It appears in Biblical Aramaic (the language of the passages in Ezra), borrowed from a vocabulary of political revolt. The word evokes the image of a conscious and deliberate action: one does not suffer a sedition, one "engages in" it, one commits it.
H0849.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both in Aramaic in the book of Ezra (4:15 and 4:19). It is set in the context of accusations made by the adversaries of Judah against the reconstruction of the temple and the city after the exile. These enemies reproach Jerusalem for a long history of rebellion against Persian authority, claiming that it is a "rebellious city" destined for destruction. The context shows that sedition is viewed as a serious political crime, worthy of royal sanction.
H0849.portee: This word reminds us that rebellion against established authority has serious and lasting consequences. For the Christian, it invites reflection on the line between just resistance to injustice and destructive rebellion, and on how accusations against God's people can be exaggerated or malicious — here, the enemies of Judah unjustly accuse the city to prevent its reconstruction.

sens: A man from the tribe of Judah during the divided monarchy
H0850.detail: Eschthon is an ancestor of the tribe of Judah, mentioned twice in 1 Chronicles 4. He is the son of Mechir and the father of Beth-Rapha, Paseach, and Tehinna. He appears in the genealogy of the descendants of Caleb, an important lineage of the tribe of Judah.
H0850.origine: The name would mean "effeminate" according to sources, but it simply designates an ancestor of the people of Judah whose memory has been preserved in the Israelite genealogies.
H0850.emploi: Eschthon appears only in 1 Chronicles 4:11-12, where he is listed in the genealogy of the descendants of Caleb. These two consecutive verses present him as the son of Mechir and the father of several men who gave their names to families or places. It is a genealogy from the time of the divided monarchy, preserved to mark the heritage of the tribe of Judah.

sens: City of Judah
Levitical city of refuge
H0851.detail:
1. Eschthemoa is a city located in the territory of Judah, mentioned in the enumeration of the cities of the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:50). It is an inhabited center that also appears in the historical accounts of the Old Testament.
2. This city has the special status of a Levitical city assigned to the sons of Aaron, the priests (1 Chronicles 6:57). It also served as a city of refuge, where someone who accidentally killed another could seek refuge. It was a place of safety and spiritual protection for the Levites in charge of divine worship.
H0851.origine: The Hebrew name אֶשְׁתְּמוֹעַ literally means "I will be heard" or "I will listen." It designates a place in the heart of the land of Judah, probably a spot where people gathered to listen or be heard. Like many city names from that era, it carries a meaning that may reflect a characteristic of the place or a founding event.
H0851.emploi: Eschthemoa appears six times in the Hebrew Bible. It is first listed among the cities of Judah (Joshua 15:50), then mentioned as a Levitical city entrusted to the sons of Aaron (Joshua 21:14 and 1 Chronicles 6:57). King David sends plunder taken from the Amalekites there (1 Samuel 30:28), showing that it was an important place during his reign. It is also linked to families of Judah in genealogies (1 Chronicles 4:17, 4:19), indicating its role in the territorial and religious organization of the kingdom.
H0851.portee: Eschthemoa reminds us that God established cities of refuge and Levitical cities for order and justice among His people. These cities symbolize divine protection and the centrality of legitimate worship in the life of Israel. They also show how God provided security for those who committed unintentional acts, reflecting His mercy toward His people.

sens: Visible mark that manifests the action of God
Prodigy or miracle accomplished by divine power
Striking testimony of God's sovereignty and majesty
H0852.detail:
1. A sign is primarily a visible mark, something that can be seen and recognized. In Daniel, these are not ordinary signs: they are extraordinary acts through which God makes Himself known. When God performs a sign, He leaves a trace of His power that all can witness (Daniel 4:2: "the signs and wonders that the Most High God has performed").

2. These signs are prodigies or miracles — events that surpass the natural order and can only be explained by direct divine intervention. They are never insignificant or secret: they are "great" and "mighty," as Daniel affirms, visible to those who see them (Daniel 4:3: "How great are His signs! How mighty are His wonders!").

3. More profoundly, a sign is a testimony of God's absolute sovereignty. It reveals who God truly is — the one who reigns eternally, who delivers, who saves, and who acts in heaven and on earth. The sign convinces and glorifies the name of God (Daniel 6:27: "He performs signs and wonders in heaven and on earth").
H0852.origine: The Hebrew word אוֹת (ot) fundamentally means "mark" or "signal" — something that draws attention and conveys a message. In Biblical Aramaic, אָת (at) is its exact form, used in the passages of the Book of Daniel. These words belong to the family of Semitic roots that designate what is visible and speaking: a sign is what is made visible to communicate the presence and power of God.
H0852.emploi: The word appears three times in Aramaic in the Book of Daniel, all in the plural, in confessions or proclamations of divine greatness. In Daniel 4:2 and 4:3, King Nebuchadnezzar acknowledges the signs and wonders performed toward him and praises God's power. In Daniel 6:27, the same king proclaims that it is the God of Daniel who performs signs and wonders. In each case, the sign is never a doubtful or ambiguous thing: it is a striking act of God that compels recognition and elicits praise. These signs are linked to God's intervention in human history to deliver, save, and manifest His eternal reign.
H0852.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that God does not act in silence or in secret: He manifests Himself through visible and powerful acts that testify to who He truly is. The signs and wonders of God are not there to satisfy curiosity, but to lead to the recognition of His sovereignty and love. By reading these passages from Daniel, one understands that God's presence in our history is never doubtful for those who have eyes to see: His acts speak clearly.

sens: Grammatical particle marking the direct object of the verb when it is defined (preceded by the article)
Simply introduces an action, process, or state without a corresponding element in the English translation
H0853.detail:
1. In Hebrew, this particle (אֵת) always introduces a direct object that is defined by the article "the." It has no equivalent in English: it is not translated, but it structures the sentence by clearly showing who or what is receiving the action. For example, in Genesis 1:16, "God made the two great lights" — the word "lights" is the object of "made," and in Hebrew this particle precedes it to highlight it. Without it, the sentence would be ambiguous.

2. This particle is so common that it structures almost all sentences with a defined object: it marks the relationship between the verb and what receives it. It adds no additional meaning, only grammatical clarity. It is a linguistic tool, like quotation marks or punctuation, without intrinsic content.
H0853.origine: This particle comes from archaic Hebrew and has the same origin as the demonstrative pronoun "that." In Aramaic, the equivalent form is יָת (yat). Its role has evolved: initially an autonomous word, it has become a simple grammatical marker essential for identifying the defined direct object. It is found in practically every Hebrew text from Genesis onward.
H0853.emploi: This particle is extremely frequent in the Hebrew Bible — it appears more than 6,700 times. It is found in all books, but is particularly abundant in the Pentateuch (the first five books), where almost every narrative sentence contains it. For example, in Genesis 1, it precedes each created creature: "God made [את] the lights," "God made [את] the animals." In 1 Samuel 20:13 and Jeremiah 19:7, it also marks the object of action or will verbs. Its usage never varies: it is always before a defined noun that receives the action.

sens: Physical proximity or joint action
Relationship or bond between people
Possession or attribute of a person
Covenant or contract established between two parties
Accompaniment or assistance in an action
H0854.detail:
1. The word primarily expresses physical proximity or joint action: two or more beings are close to each other or act together. In Genesis 7:7, Noah enters the ark "with" his wife and sons — they are physically together for this great act.
2. It describes a relationship or bond between people, such as that of companionship or friendship. In Genesis 24:40, Abraham's servant says that God walked "with" him — a benevolent and protective presence.
3. The word can indicate what a person possesses or what belongs to them: a quality, a good, an attribute. In Genesis 4:1, Eve conceives "with" the help of the Lord — she possesses this divine assistance.
4. It serves to express a covenant or pact between two parties. In Jeremiah 31:31, God announces that He will make a new covenant "with" the house of Israel — a mutual and solemn commitment.
5. It marks accompaniment or assistance: helping someone, supporting them in a task. In Exodus 18:22, the judges will carry the difficult cases "with" Moses — they assist him in his charge.
H0854.origine: This Hebrew word is a very ancient preposition, likely related to primitive Semitic forms meaning "side" or "near." It fundamentally expresses the idea of proximity or companionship. In biblical Hebrew, it is one of the most frequently used prepositions to weave relationships between people, between man and God, and to describe covenants. Its remarkable flexibility makes it an essential linguistic tool for expressing all degrees of union and relationship.
H0854.emploi: This preposition is one of the most used in the Hebrew Bible — it appears more than 800 times. It is ubiquitous from Genesis onward to express family relationships (Adam "with" Eve, Noah "with" his family), accompaniments (Abraham leaving Ur "with" his people), and especially God's covenants "with" His people. In Exodus, it expresses how God walks "with" Moses. In the Psalms, it describes the believer's communion "with" the Lord. Finally, in Jeremiah, it seals the promises of a new covenant "with" Israel. Depending on the context, it carries nuances: simple physical proximity, emotional bond, possession, solemn commitment, or mutual assistance.
H0854.portee: This small preposition opens essential truths about spiritual life. It shows that God does not leave us alone, but walks "with" us — this is the foundation of trust and faith. It also reveals that the covenant between God and His people is not a one-sided relationship, but a living companionship. For today's believer, this word invites meditation on the reality of divine presence and the gift of fraternal communion, two graces that transform existence.

sens: Pointed agricultural tool used for digging and loosening the soil
By extension, instrument of work and peace
Symbol of the conversion of war into peace
H0855.detail:
1. The hoe is a farming tool, a kind of spade or pick with a handle, used for digging, turning over, and loosening the soil before sowing. In 1 Samuel 13:20, we see the Israelites going down to the Philistines to sharpen their hoes: it is a common tool, regularly sharpened like an axe or spade, as it serves daily life.
2. The hoe also represents peaceful agricultural work and sustenance, in contrast to weapons of war. Isaiah 2:4 illustrates this well: "They shall beat their swords into plowshares," meaning that nations will transform their swords into agricultural tools, symbolizing restored peace and productive life.
3. Joel 3:10 reverses the image: "Beat your plowshares into swords" — when the threat returns, tools are reforged into weapons. The hoe thus becomes a sign of the choice between peace and war, between building and destroying.
H0855.origine: The Hebrew word אֵת (et) refers to the pointed blade of a tool, hence its meaning of hoe or pick. It comes from a root that evokes sharpness, the point. It is a very concrete word, engraved in the rural life of Israel: every farmer knew his hoe as his most useful possession.
H0855.emploi: The word appears only 5 times in biblical Hebrew, always in agricultural or symbolic contexts. 1 Samuel 13:20-21 shows it as a common tool, sharpened by Philistine craftsmen — Israel had no blacksmiths at that time. Isaiah 2:4 and Micah 4:3 (parallel passages) use it as a prophetic symbol: messianic peace will transform swords into hoes. Joel 3:10 reverses this symbol in a context of judgment: the hoe can become a weapon again. The word thus transitions from the concrete (the farmer's tool) to the symbolic (the emblem of peace or war).
H0855.portee: The hoe reminds us that true peace comes through the transformation of the heart: stopping warfare begins with choosing to cultivate, to create, to nourish. This image of swords reforged into hoes, which appears twice in prophecy (Isaiah and Micah), promises that one day Christ will establish a peace where weapons will no longer serve. It also invites us to recognize our true enemies: not men, but sin and death.

sens: king of Sidon and father of Jezebel
H0856.detail: Ethbaal is a Phoenician king of the city of Sidon, known in the Bible only because he is the father of Jezebel. His name means "with Baal," the god that the Phoenicians worshiped. Ahab, king of Israel, married Jezebel, the daughter of Ethbaal, which linked the royal house of Israel to the idolatrous customs of Phoenicia (1 Kings 16:31).
H0856.origine: The name Ethbaal (in Hebrew: 'et-ba'al) is composed of 'et ("with") and ba'al ("the master, the lord"), and particularly the god Baal. It is a typical Phoenician name, reflecting the worship of the god Baal that was central to the religion of Sidon and the Phoenician coast. The suffix -aal can also refer to the word for "lord" or "master." Historically, Ethbaal I was a king-priest of Sidon known from sources outside the Bible.
H0856.emploi: Ethbaal appears only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Kings 16:31. He is mentioned as the king of the Sidonians and father of Jezebel, the wife Ahab took. This marriage marked a serious turning point in the history of Israel: it sealed a political and religious alliance between the Northern Kingdom and idolatrous Phoenicia, introducing the worship of Baal to the royal court of Israel and opening the door to persecutions against the prophets of the Lord. Jezebel herself would become one of the most negative figures in the Bible for her fierce opposition to God.
H0856.portee: Ethbaal serves as a reminder of how marital alliances with foreign nations can lead to a serious deviation from faith. His only role in the Bible is to show us the source of Jezebel and the origin of the religious corruption that nearly destroyed God's testimony in Israel. It is a lesson on the danger of mixing faith in God with the worship of idols.

sens: To move toward a place, to arrive somewhere
To approach, to draw near (in time or space)
To occur, to happen (referring to an event)
To be brought, to be delivered (causative sense)
H0857.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of movement: coming to a place, arriving there. It is the action of moving and reaching a destination. In Isaiah 41:25, the one who is raised "has come" from the north, crossing distances. It is concrete: a person or an animal comes from point A to point B.
2. The word also means to approach, to draw near gradually, especially in time that is shortening. In Job 16:22, the number of years "touches" its end: the final moment approaches inexorably, like something that draws near to you.
3. To occur refers to the arrival of an event or calamity. It is what happens, what manifests suddenly or fatally. In Job 3:25, what one fears comes to pass; in Proverbs 1:27, terror comes like a storm.
4. The causative form (Hiphil) means to bring, to cause to come: in Isaiah 21:14, one "brings" water to the thirsty. It is the action of making something or someone arrive.
H0857.origine: The Hebrew verb אָתָה (atah) has its root in the image of movement, of what comes toward you. In Aramaic, the equivalent form אֲתָה also exists with the same meaning. The verb has no significant compounds in Hebrew, but its basic meaning (arrival, presence) dates back to the origins of the Semitic language. It is a fundamental word that simply expresses the act of coming, without particular nuance: just the movement of approach and arrival.
H0857.emploi: This verb is very frequent in the Hebrew Bible. The provided usages show it in various contexts: the arrival of God from Sinai (Deuteronomy 33:2), the coming of beasts from the fields (Isaiah 56:9), the approach of critical events or moments (Job 16:22 on the passing years, Proverbs 1:27 on terror). The verb can express both the movement of people, animals, time, and abstract events. The nuance changes little: it is always the idea of arrival, of coming closer, or of manifestation. About 20 occurrences are noted in the provided texts, especially in the prophetic and wisdom books.
H0857.portee: For the believer, this verb reminds that everything that is to come — judgment, salvation, promise — "comes" inevitably. It invites one to wait, to rely on the certain approach of God and His plans. It is also a word of hope: when the faithful is in distress or doubt, divine realities "come" to him, manifest, draw near. The verb roots faith in the real, the concrete, the eventful.

sens: to arrive, to present oneself in a place
to be brought, to be taken by someone
to bring, to take someone or something
H0858.detail:
1. To come means to arrive or to present oneself in a place. It is the movement of one who moves toward a location: Sheshbazzar "comes" to Jerusalem to lay the foundations of the temple (Ezra 5:16). In Ezra 4:12, the Jews "who have come among us" refers to their arrival in Jerusalem.
2. To be brought or taken means that one is made to come against one's will, often by order of an authority. Daniel and his companions are "brought" before King Nebuchadnezzar after his order (Daniel 3:13), just as Daniel is "brought" before King Belshazzar (Daniel 5:13).
3. To bring or take something means to make it come, to transport it to a place or a person. King Belshazzar has the gold and silver vessels from the temple "brought" to use at the table (Daniel 5:2). It is the active action of one who commands or makes the transport.
H0858.origine: The Aramaic word אֲתָה (atah) comes from the Hebrew root אָתָה (atah, "to come"), very ancient in Semitic. It simply describes the movement of one who arrives somewhere. In New Testament Greek, this Aramaic word is preserved in the liturgical phrase "Maranatha" ("Lord, come"), where it retains its sense of expectation and coming.
H0858.emploi: This Aramaic verb appears 15 times in the biblical books of Ezra and Daniel, which are partly written in Aramaic. It mainly refers to movements commanded by the kings of Babylon: bringing prisoners or captives (Ezra 5:13; Daniel 3:13; 5:13), bringing objects from the temple (Daniel 5:2; 5:3), or simply coming to accomplish a mission (Ezra 5:16). The Babylonian royal context explains the frequency of the meaning "to be brought, to be taken": it is almost always a royal order that provokes the movement. The verb is little used in a simply voluntary or free sense.
H0858.portee: This word reminds how the lives of the exiles in Babylon were subject to the orders of the king: one did not go where one wanted, but where one was "brought." It also illustrates the Christian expectation of the Lord's coming, which the Aramaic word "Maranatha" keeps alive. For the Bible reader, it is a call to pray and desire the coming of Jesus.

sens: second person singular personal pronoun, masculine, in the nominative (subject)
second person singular personal pronoun, masculine, in the accusative or genitive (object)
emphatic or highlighted form of the pronoun 'you'
H0859A.detail:
1. The pronoun 'you' refers to the person being addressed when speaking to a man or a boy. It is the subject of the verb: 'Have you eaten from the tree that I commanded you not to eat from?' (Genesis 3:11). God directly addresses Adam and holds him accountable for his disobedience.
2. The same pronoun can also be an object, following a verb or a preposition, indicating that the action pertains to the person being spoken to: 'Who told you that you were naked?' (Genesis 3:11). It is the same word, which changes grammatical role depending on its position in the sentence.
3. In Hebrew, this pronoun can also be used with particular force to emphasize or highlight: 'It is you that I choose' rather than 'I choose you.' This emphasis appears especially in direct calls or confrontations (as when Abner asks Asahel: 'Is it you?' in 2 Samuel 2:20).
H0859A.origine: Very ancient and fundamental Hebrew word. The form אַתָּה (literally: 'you') is the masculine singular form of the demonstrative personal pronoun. It is linked to a root that expresses the idea of 'this one' or 'that one,' pointing to the person being designated. It is one of the most frequent pronouns in the Hebrew Bible, used hundreds of times across all books.
H0859A.emploi: This pronoun appears 683 times in the Hebrew Bible (according to the provided count). It is omnipresent: in dialogues between God and man (Genesis 3, where God addresses Adam), in conversations between people (2 Samuel 2:20, where Abner recognizes Asahel), in prayers (Psalms 99:8, where the psalmist addresses God). Its usage varies little: it always refers to the person being spoken to. Sometimes it carries rhetorical emphasis (highlighting), especially when it concerns an accusation or identification. In wisdom and prophetic texts, it punctuates calls and exhortations.
H0859A.portee: This simple yet fundamental pronoun reminds us that the biblical word is primarily a personal and direct call. When God says 'you' to Adam, to Abraham, or to the prophet, He establishes a face-to-face, intimate, and responsible relationship. Each biblical 'you' invites the reader to feel personally addressed: it is not a distant story, but a word that speaks to you.

sens: second person singular personal pronoun, feminine, referring to a woman being directly addressed
H0859C.detail: 1. This word is simply the pronoun 'you' in Hebrew, but in the feminine singular. It is used when addressing a woman alone. For example, when Abraham says to Sarai: 'I know that you are a beautiful woman' (Genesis 12:11), he uses this feminine form because he is speaking to his wife. Similarly, in the dialogue between Elisha and the Shunammite woman, the prophet tells her 'you will have a son,' using this same form (2 Kings 4:16). It is a grammatical pronoun that simply marks the gender and number of the recipient person.
H0859C.origine: It is the feminine singular form of the personal pronoun 'you' in Hebrew (אַתָּה / atah in masculine). Hebrew, like Greek or French, distinguishes gender and number in its pronouns: one does not say 'you' the same way to a man or a woman. This distinction exists in almost all ancient languages and reflects attention to detail in communication.
H0859C.emploi: This feminine singular pronoun appears about 58 times in the Hebrew Old Testament. It is mainly found in direct dialogues, particularly in historical narratives and prophecies. It is used when someone addresses a woman directly: Abimelech to the fig tree in the fable of the trees (Judges 9:10), Elisha to the Shunammite (2 Kings 4:16), Jeremiah to the women of Israel (Jeremiah 2:27), Ezekiel to Jerusalem personified as a woman (Ezekiel 16:45). The context varies greatly, from tender to solemn, including prophetic or reproductive, but the grammatical form remains the same: it is always a pronoun addressed to a woman.

sens: second person plural personal pronoun, masculine
H0859D.detail: 1. This is the pronoun that designates a group of people being addressed, from the speaker's perspective. It can refer to a group of men or a mixed group. In Hebrew, as in French, this pronoun changes form depending on its function in the sentence (subject, object, possession), but it always refers to the same reality: the one or those to whom I am speaking. For example, when God says to Israel in Exodus 19:4 'You have seen what I did to the Egyptians,' the 'you' refers to the entire assembled people of Israel.
H0859D.origine: This word comes from the Hebrew root *at*, which expresses the idea of 'you' or 'you' as a direct recipient. There is also a singular form (אַתָּה, atta, 'you') for addressing a single person, and variations depending on the grammatical context. Aramaic, the parent language of Hebrew spoken in some regions after the exile, uses a very similar word (אַנְתּוּן, antoun) for the same meaning.
H0859D.emploi: This pronoun appears 258 times in the Hebrew Old Testament. It is found in all genres of texts: divine orders (Genesis 9:7 'You, be fruitful'), dialogues between men (Numbers 22:19 'I pray you'), laws addressed to the people (Deuteronomy 4:5 'I have taught you'), judgments (Joshua 9:23 'You are cursed'). Its usage is constant and sometimes redundant: a verb in the plural would suffice, but Hebrew states the pronoun to emphasize, draw attention, or create dramatic tension. In God's reproaches, the repetition of 'you' reinforces the tone: 'You have seen, you know' (Exodus 16:8).
H0859D.portee: This small word reminds us that God always addresses a people, never an abstraction. When God says 'you,' He speaks to living men, with their collective responsibilities and shared promises. This shows that faith is not just an individual matter: God makes a covenant with a people, gives commandments to a community, and delivers judgments to solidarity groups. The biblical 'you' invites each reader to recognize themselves in this people addressed by God.

sens: second person plural personal pronoun in the feminine, referring to a group of women or a mixed group being collectively addressed
H0859E.detail: 1. This word is the feminine plural form of the pronoun 'you' in biblical Hebrew. It addresses several women or, in some contexts, a group including women. For example, in Ezekiel 34:31, God speaks to Israel as to His sheep saying 'you, my sheep,' using this pronoun in the feminine because 'sheep' is a feminine noun in Hebrew. It is a word of pure grammar: it has no inherent meaning but serves to construct the sentence by agreeing the verb or adjective with a feminine group.
H0859E.origine: This word is a form of the personal pronoun 'you' in Hebrew (root אַתָּ֫ה / at.tah). In biblical Hebrew, as in French, pronouns change form according to their gender and number: singular or plural, masculine or feminine. This feminine plural form is regularly constructed by the grammatical rules of the ancient Hebrew language.
H0859E.emploi: This pronoun appears 5 times in the preserved texts, notably in the prophet Ezekiel. It is used whenever a divine speaker or narrator addresses a feminine group or a set designated by a feminine noun. In Genesis 31:6, Jacob says to his wives: 'You know yourselves that I have served your father.' In Ezekiel 13:11 and 13:20, God speaks to the hailstones and the cushions (feminine objects), using this pronoun to affirm that the judgment is directed at them. In Ezekiel 34:17 and 34:31, the Lord addresses the sheep (feminine) of Israel, thus marking His personal connection with His people.
H0859E.portee: This grammatical pronoun does not carry a spiritual message in itself, but its use reminds us that God's word addresses each person with personal precision: God knows whom He is addressing, man or woman, singular or group. The use of the feminine plural in Ezekiel reinforces the image of the Eternal speaking to His people as a shepherd to His sheep, with deep tenderness and intimacy.

sens: female animal of the donkey, beast of burden and riding animal
valuable property, object of material wealth
creature capable of discernment and submission to God
H0860.detail:
1. The female donkey is the female of the donkey, a robust and patient domesticated animal used for carrying loads or serving as a mount. It appears in biblical accounts as an ordinary yet valuable animal for daily life, alongside sheep and herds (Genesis 12:16; 1 Samuel 9:3).
2. The female donkey is among the material goods that signify a person's wealth. Job owned 500 female donkeys, a sign of his great prosperity (Job 1:3), and the Bible mentions female donkeys given as gifts (Genesis 45:23), showing their economic value in the eyes of ancient peoples.
3. Balaam's donkey (Numbers 22) remains the most striking example: it sees the angel of the Lord before its master, refuses to move forward, and protects Balaam from danger, then speaks wisely to divert him from the path of destruction (Numbers 22:27-32). This mute creature becomes an instrument of divine wisdom in the face of human blindness.
H0860.origine: The Hebrew word אָתוֹן (aton) is feminine, derived from the root that designates the donkey in general. Its exact etymology remains debated, but it belongs to a family of ancient words attested in several Semitic languages to name this animal. The word contrasts with סוּס (sus), the horse, which is rarer and more prestigious in the ancient Near East.
H0860.emploi: The word appears 28 times in the Old Testament, mostly in historical and wisdom narratives. It first emerges in patriarchal traditions as material wealth (Genesis 12:16; 32:15; 45:23). The episode of Balaam and his donkey (Numbers 22:21-32) is the narrative heart: faced with Balaam blinded by pride and greed, it is the animal that sees and speaks the truth. The word reappears in the story of Saul searching for his father's female donkeys (1 Samuel 9-10), which becomes the pretext for his royal anointing. Job possesses 500, symbolizing his former and restored wealth (Job 1:3; 42:12). Finally, Zechariah 9:9 prophetically mentions it, announcing that the king will come on a female donkey, not on a war horse—promise of peace and humility that the four gospels apply to Jesus.
H0860.portee: Balaam's donkey teaches an eternal lesson: the mute creature becomes a prophetess in the face of man led astray by pride. It reminds the reader that God can use any means, even the humblest, to stop one who walks toward destruction. The messianic announcement in Zechariah 9:9 reshapes the image of royalty: not the warrior power of the horse, but the humility and gentleness of one who rides a female donkey. It is a word of comfort for those who understand that true glory lies in submission to God.

sens: Furnace or very hot hearth, intended for melting metals or firing pottery
Figuratively: punishment, destruction by fire
H0861.detail:
1. The furnace is an extremely hot oven, built to reach very high temperatures to melt precious metals or fire pottery on a large scale. It is a well-known industrial or artisanal equipment in antiquity. In the account of Daniel, King Nebuchadnezzar orders the furnace to be heated "seven times more than it was appropriate to heat it" (Daniel 3:19), showing that its intensity could be increased by feeding its fire more.
2. Figuratively, the furnace symbolizes a terrible and inevitable punishment, destruction by fire. This is the fate that the king inflicts on anyone who refuses to bow down before the golden statue: to be "thrown into the midst of a burning furnace" (Daniel 3:6, 3:11, 3:15). In this context, the furnace becomes the image of divine judgment or the vengeance of power.
H0861.origine: The Hebrew word אַתּוּן (attoun) specifically designates a furnace or an oven, particularly used for industrial applications such as metallurgy or ceramics. Its etymology refers to the idea of intense heat and transformation by fire. The word appears mainly in the book of Daniel, where it takes on major symbolic importance: the furnace becomes the place where divine protection and unwavering faith are manifested.
H0861.emploi: The word appears ten times in the Hebrew Bible, all occurrences concentrated in chapter 3 of the book of Daniel. It is the famous account of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, the three young Hebrew men who refuse to worship the golden statue of King Nebuchadnezzar. The king threatens to throw them into the burning furnace (Daniel 3:6, 3:11, 3:15), then orders it to be heated excessively and to throw them in (Daniel 3:19, 3:20). The context emphasizes the extreme intensity of the fire: the soldiers who throw the three young men into the furnace are themselves consumed by the heat (Daniel 3:22). The furnace thus becomes the heart of the narrative, symbolizing both human judgment and the trial that reveals faith.
H0861.portee: This account of the furnace teaches that faithfulness to God can go through the most extreme trial, but that trust in His deliverance does not depend on the visible outcome. Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego affirm: "Our God can deliver us," while adding: "And even if He does not deliver us..." (Daniel 3:17). The furnace represents any trial or suffering that tests faith, inviting the reader to recognize that the God of Israel is sovereign even in the worst circumstances.

sens: Covered passage along a wall or building
Interior corridor of a building
Elevated space or balcony in an architectural structure
H0862B.detail:
1. A gallery is a covered passage that runs alongside a building, allowing for movement while being protected. In the vision of the temple described by Ezekiel, these galleries form corridors all around the sanctuary (Ezekiel 41:15 and 41:16), creating organized circulation around the main edifice.
2. The word also designates structured interior spaces on multiple levels. In the temple, there are galleries on the first, second, and third floors (Ezekiel 42:3), which reduce the available space on the upper floors by overhanging the lower levels (Ezekiel 42:5), somewhat like internal balconies or mezzanines.
3. In the context of the temple, these galleries serve to delineate space and organize the different sacred areas around the central sanctuary.
H0862B.origine: The Hebrew word אַתִּיק (attiq) comes from a root that evokes the idea of what surrounds or encircles. It belongs to the architectural vocabulary of ancient Hebrew and specifically designates passages or spaces that conform to the contours of a building. This technical term appears almost exclusively in architectural descriptions of the temple.
H0862B.emploi: The word appears four times, solely in the detailed description of the temple given by the prophet Ezekiel in chapters 41 and 42. Ezekiel meticulously enumerates the dimensions and layout of the visionary temple: the galleries are mentioned as structural elements that encircle the building at multiple levels. They play a role in spatial organization, notably by reducing the dimensions of the upper chambers. It is a purely architectural word, limited to the vocabulary of the description of the sanctuary.
H0862B.portee: These galleries of the visionary temple remind us that divine worship is an organized and intentional act. Every architectural detail expresses an order established by God.
