For the believer, this description invites contemplation of divine wisdom and precision, even in the material elements of the place of encounter with God.

sens: Foreign warrior from Gath in the service of King David
Military leader of David during Absalom's rebellion
Model of unconditional loyalty to the king
H0863G.detail:
1. Ittaï is a military officer from Gath, a Philistine city, who serves in the army of King David. Although a foreigner, he earns the trust and authority of the king.
2. During Absalom's rebellion, David entrusts Ittaï with the command of one third of the army, alongside Joab and Abishai (2 Samuel 18:2). He plays a strategic role in suppressing the rebellion.
3. Ittaï embodies total loyalty: when David considers sending him away before the battle, he declares, "Wherever my lord the king goes, whether for death or for life, there also will your servant be" (2 Samuel 15:21), showing that he will never abandon him.
H0863G.origine: The name Ittaï literally means "with me" in Hebrew (the root expresses companionship and closeness). This etymology perfectly reflects his role: a man who faithfully stands by the king in difficult times. His title, "of Gath," indicates his foreign origin, which makes his loyalty to David all the more remarkable.
H0863G.emploi: Ittaï appears exclusively in the account of David's flight from Absalom (2 Samuel 15-18). David first meets him in 2 Samuel 15:19 and dismisses him out of respect for his status as a foreigner. But Ittaï refuses to leave, declaring that he will remain loyal regardless of the circumstances (2 Samuel 15:21). David then accepts his presence. Later, Ittaï receives command of troops as one of David's three generals (2 Samuel 18:2), where he is ordered by the king to spare young Absalom (2 Samuel 18:5). His presence among the military leaders shows that he has gained a position of trust and significant responsibility.
H0863G.portee: Ittaï illustrates unconditional loyalty and sincere devotion. His refusal to abandon David in times of crisis, despite being a foreigner and having reasons to leave, teaches what it means to be loyal out of conviction and not personal interest. For the Christian reader, his example evokes the call to follow the Lord "whether for death or for life," in all circumstances, without calculation or reservation.

sens: Warrior of David, from Gibeah in the territory of Benjamin
H0863H.detail: Ittaï is one of the thirty mighty men of King David, listed among the greatest warriors of Israel. He is the son of Ribai and hails from Gibeah, a city in the territory of the tribe of Benjamin. His name literally means "with me," which may reflect his role as a faithful companion of the king. He appears in two parallel sources: 2 Samuel 23:29 and 1 Chronicles 11:31, where he is sometimes called Ithaï. These lists of warriors illustrate the diversity of the men who made up David's elite army, coming from different regions of Israel.
H0863H.origine: The name Ittaï means "with me" in Hebrew. This meaning expresses the idea of closeness and companionship, which is particularly fitting for a trusted warrior by the king's side. The name evokes the loyalty and solidarity that bound these men to David.
H0863H.emploi: Ittaï is mentioned twice in the Bible, both times in lists of renowned warriors. He first appears in 2 Samuel 23:29 among David's thirty mighty men, presented as the son of Ribai from Gibeah, in the territory of Benjamin. The same mention is found in 1 Chronicles 11:31, where he sometimes bears the slightly different name of Ithaï. These two parallel passages highlight his status as a recognized warrior in King David's military administration, without providing further biographical details.
H0863H.portee: Ittaï's presence in the list of David's thirty mighty men reminds us that the king does not surround himself only with men from his own tribe, but recruits the best warriors from all of Israel, including from the northern territories. This diversity illustrates how God unites different tribes and regions around a common purpose.

sens: Stage in the desert where Israel camped after leaving Egypt
Location at the edge of the desert, between Succoth and Pi-Hahiroth
H0864.detail:
1. Étham is the name of a place where the people of Israel stopped during their exodus from Egypt. After leaving Succoth, the Israelites camped there at the beginning of their long journey to the Promised Land (Exodus 13:20). It was an important stage in the journey, marking the transition from the inhabited area to the desert region.

2. Geographically, Étham was located at the edge of the desert, between Succoth and Pi-Hahiroth (Numbers 33:7). This place served as a starting point or passage in the desert itself: the text mentions "the desert of Étham" as a region where the Israelites traveled for three days (Numbers 33:8). It was therefore a transitional area, marking the boundary between the civilized world and the vast desert.
H0864.origine: The name Étham means "with them" or "their plow" according to ancient sources, although its exact etymology remains debated by scholars. It designates a strategic location in Sinai, a recognizable landmark on the route of the Exodus. The name appears only in the accounts of the Exodus and in the enumeration of the stages of the journey (Book of Numbers).
H0864.emploi: Étham is mentioned four times, exclusively in the books of Exodus and Numbers. It first appears in Exodus 13:20 as the first stage in the desert after leaving Egypt. The other three mentions (Numbers 33:6, 33:7, 33:8) are part of the systematic enumeration of Israel's encampments during the forty years of wandering in the desert. This enumeration reiterates and specifies the route: it is from Étham that the people "turned back toward Pi-Hahiroth" and undertook the crossing of the Red Sea. Étham thus marks the boundary between Egypt and the great desert, and the beginning of the spectacular divine intervention.
H0864.portee: Étham reminds the reader that the Exodus was a true journey: not a chaotic flight, but an orderly itinerary where God guided His people step by step. This detail about the name of a small camping place underscores that God knows and accompanies each of our steps, each of our stages, no matter how modest they may be. It is a call to trust in God's path, even when entering the unknown of the desert.

sens: The day that immediately preceded today
A time that has passed, expired, prior to the present moment
Before an action or state being discussed
H0865.detail:
1. The primary meaning is literal: yesterday, the day that comes just before today. This is what the psalmist says when he mentions how "a thousand years in your sight are like a day that has just gone by" (Psalms 90:4): for God, even a millennium passes as quickly as a day that is gone.
2. Figuratively, the word denotes a past time, expired, without precision on its distance: formerly, once, in ancient times. When David questions Saul, he "was like before" (1 Samuel 19:7), meaning in the previous state where Saul loved him. Similarly, 2 Samuel 5:2 recalls that "formerly, when Saul was king, it was you who led Israel."
3. The word can also indicate continuity or repetition: "like before" means "as it was, as it used to be." Thus, 1 Samuel 14:21 describes how the Hebrews "like before" joined Israel: they acted as they did previously.
H0865.origine: The Hebrew word אֶתְמוֹל is formed from the root תמל ("yesterday") and the prefix אֶת ("accusative marker"), which reinforces the sense of something that is expired, finished. It is a word that expresses the past through the image of time that has elapsed: yesterday is always behind us, inaccessible. The image is that of a day that has disappeared, of what is no longer, hence the figurative meaning of "ancient," "past," "formerly."
H0865.emploi: This word appears eight times in the Hebrew Bible. It is used mainly in the historical books (1 and 2 Samuel, once in Psalm 90, and once in the Prophets). Its meaning varies according to the context: in 1 Samuel 4:7 and 10:11, it marks a comparison with the immediate past ("up to now," "before"). In 1 Samuel 14:21 and 19:7, it indicates a previous state or situation that persists or serves as a reference ("like before"). In 2 Samuel 5:2, it evokes a more distant past, more clearly "formerly." The word can thus denote the day of yesterday, but also anything that is simply expired, near or far.
H0865.portee: This word reminds the reader that time flows, that the present becomes past, and that God alone reigns over this temporal flow. For the Christian faith, it invites one to turn toward what remains and does not pass away. By reading that God sees a thousand years as a day that has gone by, the believer is directed to God's eternity and the fragility of human time.

sens: Payment in money or goods given in exchange for a service or work
Price or reward that is dishonest, obtained through reprehensible acts
H0866.detail:
1. Salary is what one receives in return for work or a service rendered. It is a regular or agreed compensation, intended to pay the one who works. In Hosea 2:14, the term refers to the gifts that lovers gave to the unfaithful woman — she called them her "salaries," as if they were the normal price of a transaction.
2. The word can also describe a gain or a dishonest reward, obtained through a reprehensible or shameful act. The context of Hosea 2 clearly shows this: these "salaries" are received from lovers in exchange for infidelity. This meaning emphasizes the immoral or unworthy nature of what is received.
H0866.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root evoking the idea of fixing, concluding an agreement or transaction. It is related to other Hebrew words denoting commercial arrangements or exchanges. The basic image is that of a fixed and agreed compensation — something that is negotiated or exchanged.
H0866.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Hosea 2:14. It describes the gifts that lovers give to an unfaithful woman. The prophet Hosea uses this term with irony and condemnation: these gifts are presented as "salaries" to highlight the transactional and shameful nature of the relationship. The prophetic context makes it a symbol of the infidelity of the people of Israel toward God.
H0866.portee: This word shows us how the Bible speaks frankly about dark moral realities. By calling these gifts "salaries," Hosea does not hide the sinful nature of the transaction: he names it, judges it. For the Christian reader, this reminds us that everything we receive — our resources, our talents, our blessings — comes from God, and that placing them elsewhere or using them wrongly is a form of serious infidelity.

sens: Levite from the time of the divided monarchy, ancestor of Asaph
H0867.detail: Ethni is a man from the tribe of Levi mentioned in the genealogy of the Temple musicians during the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided into two rival kingdoms. He appears in the lineage that traces back to Asaph, the choir leader of King David. His name means "my reward" in Hebrew, and he is the father of Malchijah.
H0867.origine: The name Ethni literally means "my reward" (from the Hebrew root evoking salary or compensation). In 1 Chronicles 6:41, he is also called Jeatherai, which shows that this name is a variant or nickname. He is among the ancestors of the Levitical musical clan, which explains his inclusion in the official genealogy of the Temple.
H0867.emploi: Ethni is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 6:41, in the midst of a detailed genealogical list of Levites responsible for the music of worship at the Temple. This mention is part of the narrative of the restoration of divine service after the Ark of the Covenant was brought to Jerusalem. His rank in the genealogy (son of Zerah, father of Malchijah) shows that he held an important place in the transmission of Levitical service.

sens: Price that a prostitute receives for her acts
Money earned through prostitution or idolatry
Shameful and cursed remuneration by God
H0868.detail:
1. The word denotes the price received by a prostitute for her services. It is a salary like any other, but marked by infamy: Deuteronomy 23:18 forbids bringing it to the temple of God. The image is that of a commercial transaction, but degrading.
2. The Bible also uses this word to figuratively describe the income of a nation that engages in idolatry. Isaiah 23:17-18 speaks of the gain that Tyre derives from its prostitution, meaning that the city, like a sold woman, prostitutes itself to false powers. It is a powerful way to show that religious infidelity is a form of shameful commerce.
3. In both cases, this salary is marked by a curse: the Lord abhors it, and the Bible marks it with the seal of the impure and the repugnant. It is an income that God rejects and that cannot be offered to Him.
H0868.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of payment or remuneration. It is specifically used for the salary of prostitution, which distinguishes it from ordinary words for "salary" or "wages." This specialization of meaning shows how the biblical language charges this word with a moral condemnation from the outset.
H0868.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost always in a context of condemnation. Deuteronomy 23:18 establishes the fundamental prohibition: this salary must not cross the threshold of the temple. In the prophets (Isaiah, Ezekiel, Hosea, Micah), the word becomes a metaphor for idolatry: Jerusalem and Tyre, once faithful cities, are depicted as prostitutes who earn their bread by engaging with foreign powers and false gods. Ezekiel 16:31-34 plays on this word cruelly: while ordinary prostitutes receive a salary, Jerusalem, in its perversion, pays for its lovers — it is therefore worse than an ordinary prostitute. The word always carries a charge of shame and abomination.
H0868.portee: This word reminds us that God does not tolerate the price of sexual sin or idolatry being presented to Him as an offering. It teaches us that certain gains are tainted with shame from their source, and that money earned through evil cannot become legitimate by being religiously consecrated. For a nation or a church, this word warns: when the community turns away from God to seek power or security elsewhere, it prostitutes itself, and the fruits of this infidelity can only lead to ruin.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah during the time of the divided monarchy
H0869.detail: Ethnan is a man of the tribe of Judah mentioned only once in the Old Testament. He is the son of Ashhur and Helea, and the brother of several other men: Haahashtari, Zerah, Izhar, and Koz. He also has half-brothers, Ahuzzam, Hepher, and Temeni. His name literally means "wage of impurity" in ancient Hebrew, an expression that evokes the price paid for an act contrary to God's law. Like many other genealogies of the tribe of Judah, Ethnan is known to us only through this genealogical list preserved in the first book of Chronicles (1 Chronicles 4:7).
H0869.origine: The name Ethnan comes from Hebrew and literally means "wage of impurity" or "price of prostitution." It is composed of two elements: "et" (wage, price, remuneration) and "nan" (dishonesty, impurity). This type of name, quite dark in its meaning, was sometimes given in ancient families without determining the destiny of the person who bore it.
H0869.emploi: Ethnan appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:7, where he is listed among the sons of Ashhur and Helea, in a genealogy of the tribe of Judah. This genealogy places Ethnan in the time of the divided monarchy, that is, after the division of the kingdom of Israel into two kingdoms. There is no other information about his deeds or life: the biblical text simply names him in this family list.

sens: Specific place, position in space
Location where something was or should be
Vestige, trace of a past presence
What comes after, succession in time
H0870.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning is that of a place, a position in physical space. It is the spot, the point of location: "Let the house of God be rebuilt on the place where it was" (Ezra 5:15) refers to the exact location where the temple once stood.
2. The word also designates the precise location occupied by something — the site, the place where objects must be restored or rebuilt. In Ezra 6:5, the gold and silver utensils must be "returned, transported to the temple in Jerusalem to the place where they were."
3. A trace, a vestige: what remains of a presence, an action. After the stone reduced the statue to dust, "no trace was found" (Daniel 2:35), meaning no mark, no visible remains.
4. The word also takes on a temporal meaning: what comes after, the succession. "After you, another kingdom will arise" (Daniel 2:39) marks a sequence, what happens in the course of time.
H0870.origine: The Hebrew word אֲתַר comes from a root that evokes the trace, the imprint left by a passage. It is related to the notion of "following" or "coming after." In Aramaic (the language of the Targum and some biblical passages), it retains this sense of place or location. The word aligns with the idea of what persists or remains: a stable location, a mark of the past.
H0870.emploi: This word appears 8 times in biblical Aramaic, concentrated in the books of Ezra and Daniel, texts that deal with the restoration of the temple and prophetic visions. In Ezra (5:15 to 6:7), it systematically designates the location of the temple in Jerusalem and the position of the objects that belong there — it is about restoring a space and goods to their original place. In Daniel (2:35 and 2:39), the word shifts to broader meanings: the trace of a destroyed reality and the chronological succession of kingdoms. It is a term that the Bible uses to establish locations and orders.
H0870.portee: For the reader, this word reminds us of the biblical importance of place: God chose a specific location, Jerusalem and its temple, where His presence is manifested. The restoration of the temple on its ancient site (Ezra) emphasizes that God honors what He has consecrated and brings His people back to their rightful place. The word also tells us that history has an order, a sequence that God controls (Daniel), and that even ruin leaves traces of the past that God remembers.

sens: Passage or route in the desert of the Negev
H0871.detail: 1. Atharim designates a path or mountain passage through which Israel passed in the Negev region, south of Canaan, during its return from Egypt. The king of Arad learns by this path that Israel is approaching Canaan and attacks the people of God (Numbers 21:1).
H0871.origine: The Hebrew word אֲתָרִים (atharim) likely means "mountain passage" or "caravan route." It possibly comes from a root that refers to the idea of crossing or passing. It is a specific place name in the desert of the Negev, in southern Canaan.
H0871.emploi: Atharim appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 21:1. It is a strategic passage in the desert through which Israel was transiting. The context indicates that this path was known to the inhabitants of Canaan, as the king of Arad learned of Israel's approach by this route. This passage then becomes the starting point for an attack against the Israelites.

sens: The passage through which one enters a place, a door or access
The very act of entering, the movement of entry
The threshold or point of crossing into a space
H0872.detail:
1. The word designates the physical opening through which one enters a place: it is the door or passage. In Ezekiel 8:5, the entrance of the temple is the specific place where an idol stands, marking a sacred threshold that has been violated.
2. It can also refer to the very act of entering, the moment or movement of passage — the act of crossing a threshold rather than the threshold itself.
3. By extension, the word evokes the idea of beginning or access: it is through the entrance that one enters and begins to penetrate a new space.
H0872.origine: The Hebrew word בִּאָה comes from the root בוא (ba' : "to go, to come, to enter"). It particularly designates the entrance or access — the place or act of arrival. This root is very common in biblical Hebrew to express movement inward or the approach to a place.
H0872.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 8:5, where it designates the northern entrance of the temple in Jerusalem. In this prophetic context, Ezekiel sees an idol placed precisely at this entrance, symbolizing the profanation of the sanctuary and the entry of idolatry into the holy place. The usage here is very concrete: it refers to a specific architectural location, the physical access to the temple.
H0872.portee: This word reminds us that each entrance — each threshold we cross — can become a place of moral decision. The presence of the idol at the entrance of the temple symbolizes how sin often begins at the door, before penetrating further. For the Christian reader, it is an invitation to be vigilant about what enters their life from the very beginning, from the outermost thresholds.

sens: Morally bad, contrary to justice and righteousness
Causing harm, harmful, pernicious
Unpleasant, repugnant in a physical sense
H0873.detail:
1. The word designates what is morally bad, contrary to divine justice and righteousness. In Ezra 4:12, the rebellious city of Jerusalem is called "wicked" because it stands against the authority of the king: it represents a revolt, a guilty insubordination.
2. It also applies to what is harmful and pernicious, to what causes harm. A wicked city is dangerous to the established power: its restored walls and foundations are feared as a threat.
3. The word carries the image of what is repugnant or unpleasant: it comes from a root that evokes a foul odor, showing that evil offends and deeply disgusts.
H0873.origine: The Aramaic word comes from the Hebrew verb בָּאַשׁ (ba.ash), which literally means "to smell bad" or "to stink." This sensory root — the foul smell — gradually becomes an image of moral evil: what smells bad is repulsive, disgusting, abominable. Biblical Aramaic borrows this root to express the repugnant nature of evil.
H0873.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 4:12, in the official correspondence addressed to the king of Persia. The local authorities denounce the Jews rebuilding Jerusalem, calling it a "wicked" city — that is, rebellious and dangerous to the established order. The context shows that this is a political and moral accusation: a revolt against legitimate authority is perceived as profoundly evil and intolerable.
H0873.portee: This term reminds us that the Bible evaluates actions and attitudes in light of divine justice. A revolt against God's law, even disguised under a political facade, is always "wicked" in the eyes of the Lord. For the believer, this invites examination of whether their own obedience to God is authentic, beyond appearances.

sens: Make clear and distinct, highlight
Engrave clearly, trace letters or words visibly
H0874.detail:
1. Make clear and distinct, highlight. The verb designates the action of bringing something out so that it is well understood. Moses "explains" the law to the people of Israel (Deuteronomy 1:5), meaning he develops it, presenting it in a way that everyone grasps what it requires.
2. Engrave clearly, trace letters or words visibly. The word also applies to writing engraved on stone or tablets. The words must be "engraved clearly" on the stones (Deuteronomy 27:8), and the prophecy must be "engraved" on tablets (Habakkuk 2:2), so that it can be read clearly without ambiguity.
H0874.origine: The verb comes from a root that evokes the idea of making visible and distinct. In Hebrew, this verb in the Piel form (which intensifies the action) means to highlight, to make manifest. The basic image is that of tracing or marking something in a way that makes it stand out, making it impossible to ignore or misinterpret.
H0874.emploi: The verb appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always with the meaning of clarifying or marking clearly. Moses uses it in Deuteronomy 1:5 to say that he will clearly present the law to the people. In Deuteronomy 27:8, the term applies to the inscription engraved on the stones of the covenant: the words must be written "clearly," without blur. In Habakkuk 2:2, the prophet is commanded to engrave the vision on tablets, so that it can be easily read. The word always expresses this idea of clarity and visibility, whether it is that of well-explained oral discourse or of easily readable writing.
H0874.portee: This word reminds us that God wants His word to be clearly understood. Whether read in the law given to Moses or in a prophecy, it must be clear, accessible, engraved indelibly. For the believer, this emphasizes the importance of scrutinizing Scripture diligently and transmitting it without obscuring it.

sens: Pit dug in the ground to draw water
Opening, deep cavity in the ground
Water springing from the earth, source
Image of what gives life or allows survival
Image of depth and danger
H0875.detail:
1. The well is a hole intentionally dug to reach underground water, essential in the dry regions of the Middle East. Genesis 24:11 shows the women coming to draw water at the well at fixed times; Genesis 29:2-3 describes the flocks being watered at this same well, covered by a large stone.
2. The word also designates the dug opening, the pit itself: in Genesis 14:10, the valley of Siddim is "covered with wells" of bitumen, where enemy kings fall; in 2 Samuel 17:19, one can cover the opening of the well to hide it.
3. By extension, it means the spring that gushes forth, the water that naturally comes from the earth (Numbers 21:17-18 speaks of the well that gushed forth).
4. The well becomes an image of life and satisfaction: Proverbs 5:15 invites one to drink from their own well, meaning to enjoy what belongs to them; Song of Solomon 4:15 compares the beloved to a well of life.
5. It can also symbolize danger and death: Psalms 69:16 speaks of falling into the deep pit, an image of despair and judgment.
H0875.origine: The Hebrew word בְּאֵר (beer) derives from a root meaning "to dig" or "to unearth." It is very ancient and universal: all Mediterranean and Middle Eastern peoples depended on wells. The word belongs to the same family as verbs describing drilling and digging. In Aramaic, a similar form is found. It is a very common word that needs little explanation: every Israelite knew that a well was a vital, everyday reality, especially in the desert.
H0875.emploi: The word appears 34 times in the Bible, mainly in Genesis and the early chapters of Exodus, where water is a constant issue. Wells dominate the stories of Abraham and Isaac: in Genesis 21 and 26, Isaac digs wells and disputes with the Philistines over their possession, showing their value. In Genesis 24, Abraham's servant meets Rebecca at the well, a detail that underscores the importance of the place as a public space. Moses flees near a well (Exodus 2:15). On the way to the Promised Land, the well becomes a symbol: Numbers 21:16-18 recounts the song of the well, where water miraculously gushes forth to quench the people's thirst. Proverbs and Psalms use it figuratively: a source of inner life, depth of heart or danger.
H0875.portee: The well reminds us that water — a symbol of life, grace, and the Spirit — does not spring forth spontaneously; it must be sought, sometimes laboriously dug. It is also an image of security and abundance in an arid desert: whoever possesses a well possesses life. In a spiritual sense, Jesus speaks to the Samaritan woman of living water that springs up to eternal life (John 4), renewing this ancient image of the well. The well also speaks of sharing: a well calls for community, gathering, and mutual aid.

sens: Stopping place where the Israelites received water during the Exodus
H0876G.detail: Beer is an oasis in the desert where the people of Israel stopped during their wandering in the desert, after leaving Egypt. It is there that God promised Moses to give water to the thirsty people (Numbers 21:16). The very name means "well" in Hebrew, which recalls the crucial importance of this water source in the arid desert.
H0876G.origine: The word בְּאֵר (be.er) comes from the Hebrew root meaning "well" or "spring." This descriptive name evokes the image of a well or oasis, that is, a point of water springing from the ground, essential for life in the desert. The well was for the ancients a symbol of life and salvation in arid lands.
H0876G.emploi: Beer appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 21:16, in the account of the people's journey through the desert. This stop occurs after victories against the Amorites and constitutes a moment of encouragement: God responds to the people's thirst by promising water. This account is part of the series of wonders that God performs to sustain His people during the Exodus.
H0876G.portee: Beer reminds the reader that God provides for the needs of His people in the desert, not out of lack of compassion but through His promises. It is a testimony of divine faithfulness to those who follow Him, even in times of distress and deprivation.

sens: City located west of Hebron, in the Holy Land
H0876H.detail: Beer is a city mentioned only once in the Bible, in the account of Jotham fleeing from his brother Abimelech. It is there that Jotham takes refuge to ensure his safety, away from the one who massacred his brothers.
H0876H.origine: The name Beer literally means "well" in Hebrew (from the word בְּאֵר = "well"). This city bears a name that evokes water and the essential resources for life in the desert. Beer may be another name for Beeroth (בְּאֵרוֹת), a city of the Gibeonites.
H0876H.emploi: Beer appears only once in the Bible, in Judges 9:21, as a place of refuge. Jotham, the sole survivor of the massacre perpetrated by Abimelech, flees there to escape his brother. This mention underscores the importance of this city as a sufficiently distant and safe place to shelter a fugitive.

sens: Reservoir dug in rock or soil to collect and store water
Figuratively, source of spiritual nourishment or blessing
Figuratively, pretense or vain promise
H0877.detail:
1. A cistern is a well or basin dug into the ground to collect rainwater or store it. In the Holy Land, where water is precious and rare, cisterns are essential facilities for daily life. David asks his men to bring him water from the cistern near Bethlehem (2 Samuel 23:15-16), which shows how valued this water was.

2. God describes Himself as a "fountain of living water" in contrast to human cisterns (Jeremiah 2:13). The image evokes that God offers abundant and overflowing life, while everything sought elsewhere runs dry and is exhausted.

3. The "broken cisterns" of Jeremiah 2:13 symbolize false promises and useless sources: they promise to hold water but let it escape. This is the image of everything one hopes in without God — it never satisfies.
H0877.origine: The Hebrew word בֹּאר comes from a root meaning "to dig" or "to pierce." It literally designates a hole dug to draw and store water. The cistern is the product of human labor, unlike the spring that flows by itself. This contrast between the cistern (what is made) and the living water (what God gives) is at the heart of the prophetic imagery in Jeremiah.
H0877.emploi: The word appears three times in the provided usages, always referring to a concrete reality or a spiritual image. In 2 Samuel 23:15-16, it refers to the historical cistern of Bethlehem, from which David's warriors draw precious water. In Jeremiah 2:13, the prophet uses the word twice in the same sentence to describe Israel's idolatry: the people abandon God, the living source, to dig cisterns that cannot hold water. This image links the concrete meaning and the spiritual meaning: just as a broken cistern cannot satisfy thirst, false gods cannot satisfy the soul.
H0877.portee: This biblical image reminds Christians that seeking satisfaction outside of God — in material goods, pleasures, power, or false teachings — is like drinking from sources that never satisfy. Only God, the fountain of living water, can truly quench spiritual thirst. It invites the reader to examine where they draw meaning and joy in their life.

sens: Man from the tribe of Asher during the divided monarchy
H0878.detail: Beera is a man from the tribe of Asher, mentioned only once in the Bible. He appears in the genealogy of his tribe in 1 Chronicles 7:37, listed among the sons of Zophah. He was a contemporary during the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided between the northern kingdom (Israel) and the southern kingdom (Judah).
H0878.origine: The name Beera literally means "a well." This meaning evokes the gushing water, source of life and abundant life in the context of the ancient Near East where water was precious.
H0878.emploi: Beera appears only once in the Scriptures: in 1 Chronicles 7:37. He is listed in the detailed genealogy of the tribe of Asher, where the names of his brothers are enumerated. No particular event or action is reported about him; he is simply recorded in the genealogical history of his people.

sens: Well located in southern Moab
H0879.detail: 1. Eglaim is a water well in the region of southern Moab, territory east of the Dead Sea. Its Hebrew name literally means "well of God" (Beer = well, Elim = God). This place serves as a geographical landmark in the Bible to designate a boundary or area of the Moabite land.
H0879.origine: The name Eglaim comes from two Hebrew words: "beer" which means "well" or "water source," and "elim" which designates God. It is a common compound name in Hebrew for places related to water and the sacred. The well was likely an important facility for life in an arid region.
H0879.emploi: Eglaim appears only once in the Bible, in the book of Isaiah in chapter 15. The prophet describes divine judgment on Moab: the cries and lamentations of the Moabite people resound to Eglaim, this well in the southern part of the land. This precise geographical detail shows that desolation extends from one end of the territory to the other, from north to south.

sens: Leader of the tribe of Reuben during the divided monarchy
H0880.detail: Beera is a Reubenite leader who lived at the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided into two kingdoms. He is the son of Baal and was taken captive to Assyria by King Tiglath-Pileser, as reported in 1 Chronicles 5:6.
H0880.origine: The name Beera means "well" in Hebrew, composed of two elements: bé- ("well") and -éra. This name may reflect an image of wells, a symbol of life and resource in the Israeli desert. Beera belongs to the genealogy of the tribe of Reuben, whose history is traced in chapter 5 of 1 Chronicles.
H0880.emploi: Beera appears only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 5:6. He is presented as a prince of the Reubenites, a descendant of Baal. His historicity is confirmed by his forced exile in Assyria, likely during the conquest campaigns of King Tiglath-Pileser in the 8th century BC. This passage fits into the genealogy of Reuben and illustrates the dispersion of the northern Israelites by the Assyrian empires.

sens: City of Canaan allotted to the tribe of Benjamin
Gibeonite city allied with Israel at the time of Joshua
Inhabited center from which descendants came after the exile
H0881G.detail:
1. Beéroth was a city in Canaan, one of the four Gibeonite cities (Gibeon, Kephira, Beéroth, and Kirjath-Jearim) that made an alliance with Israel during the conquest of the land (Joshua 9:17). Its name means "well" in Hebrew, evoking a location with water sources. It was assigned to the tribe of Benjamin during the division of the territory (Joshua 18:25).
2. Beéroth played an administrative and political role in the Benjaminite region. In 2 Samuel 4:2, we learn that it was an important enough center to host military leaders of Saul's kingdom and was clearly identified as belonging to Benjamin.
3. After the Babylonian exile, descendants of the inhabitants of Beéroth returned to Judea with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:25 and Nehemiah 7:29), forming a community of seven hundred forty-three people, which shows its demographic importance at the time of the return.
H0881G.origine: The Hebrew name בְּאֵרוֹת (beérot) is the plural of בְּאֵר (béer), which means "well" or "spring." This descriptive name reflects the geography of the region: a place characterized by the presence of water, an essential resource in the arid climate of Canaan. The name thus reveals the natural conditions of the site and its strategic importance for the inhabitants.
H0881G.emploi: Beéroth is mentioned five times in the Bible. It first appears in the Gibeonite alliance with Joshua (Joshua 9:17), then in the list of Benjaminite cities during the division of the territory (Joshua 18:25). It resurfaces in 2 Samuel 4:2 as the origin point of characters from the royal period, confirming its continuity of occupation. Finally, it appears twice in the lists of returnees after the exile (Ezra 2:25 and Nehemiah 7:29), always alongside the same Gibeonite cities, highlighting the geographical and administrative stability of the Benjaminite territory through the centuries.
H0881G.portee: Beéroth reminds us how the Lord allowed a small group of Canaanites, the Gibeonites, to survive and integrate into Israel through a loyal treaty, becoming a lasting part of the community. Its history also illustrates God's faithfulness in bringing families from this city back from exile, showing that even the minor cities of the promised land have their place in God's plan for return and restoration.

sens: Location in the territory of Benjamin during the conquest of Canaan
H0881H.detail: 1. Beéroth-Bené is a compound name: "Beéroth" literally means "the wells" (from the Hebrew word meaning "well"), and "Bené" means "the sons of." This location was assigned to the tribe of Benjamin during the division of the conquered territory. It is mentioned in Deuteronomy 10:6 as a stopping point on the Israelites' journey in the desert, where the people stopped after leaving other sites: it is here that Aaron, the high priest, died and was buried.
H0881H.origine: The name is formed from two Hebrew elements: "bé-éroth" ("the wells") and "bené Yaakan" ("the sons of Jaakan"). Yaakan was an Edomite chief, and this compound geographical name reflects either the importance of water sources in this place or a historical association with this group. The first element recalls the vital importance of water in the desert and the arid territories of Canaan.
H0881H.emploi: This name appears only once in the provided Bible, in Deuteronomy 10:6. It is a landmark in the route of the people of Israel after the exodus from Egypt, located on the way to Canaan. The mention of Aaron's death in this place makes it symbolically important: it is where the ministry of the first high priest ends, and where his son Eleazar succeeds him. This locality also appears in the lists of Gibeonite cities assigned to Benjamin.

sens: Hittite father of Judith, wife of Esau
H0882G.detail: Beéri is a Hittite man whose daughter Judith became one of Esau's wives (Genesis 26:34). He appears only once in the patriarchal narrative, identified simply by his lineage.
H0882G.origine: The name Beéri means "my well" in Hebrew (beer = well). It is a meaningful name that evokes wealth and life in the desert, where wells are precious. Beéri is a Hittite name mentioned during the time of the patriarchs, when the Hittites inhabited Canaan.
H0882G.emploi: Beéri appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 26:34, where he is presented as the father of Judith, a Hittite woman whom Esau took as a wife at the age of forty. This passage situates Beéri among the Canaanite inhabitants of the patriarchal period and shows the marital alliances between the descendants of Abraham and the local peoples.

sens: father of the prophet Hosea
H0882H.detail: Beéri is the father of the prophet Hosea. His name means "my well" in Hebrew. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Hosea 1:1, where he is identified as the father of Hosea, the prophet to whom God spoke during the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah in Judah, and Jeroboam in Israel.
H0882H.origine: The name Beéri comes from Hebrew and literally means "my well." The root "bĕ'ēr" refers to a well, and the suffix "-î" expresses possession ("my"). It is a theophoric name that reflects trust in God as the source of life and provision.
H0882H.emploi: Beéri appears only once in the Bible, in Hosea 1:1. He is identified there as the father of the prophet Hosea, to whom God addressed his words during the period of the divided monarchy. Although not detailed, this single usage situates Hosea in a specific historical and familial context, allowing the reader to understand that the prophet came from a family in northern Israel.
H0882H.portee: Beéri reminds us that God's prophets did not arise from nothing: they had a familial and historical grounding. The simple fact that Beéri is named as the father of Hosea shows the importance that the Bible places on genealogy and spiritual heritage. This invites us to recognize that God can raise up men of faith from any family and era.

sens: Well located west of Kadesh, south of Israel
H0883.detail: 1. Well located west of Kadesh, south of Israel: It is a well-localized geographical place in the Negev desert, where Hagar meets the angel of God and receives the promise of a descendant (Genesis 16:14). Isaac stays there after fleeing the sacrifice and dwells there for a long time (Genesis 24:62; Genesis 25:11).
H0883.origine: The name means in Hebrew "well of the one who sees me" or "well of the Living who sees me." It combines three words: Be'er (well), La-Haï (of the Living), and Roï (who sees me). It is a theophanic name — it celebrates Hagar's miraculous encounter with the Angel of the Lord, who reveals to her that God sees her in her distress.
H0883.emploi: This well appears three times in Genesis, always in southern Canaan. Hagar names it thus after her divine vision (Genesis 16:14); Isaac resides there in the Negev (Genesis 24:62) and it is near there that he lives when Abraham dies (Genesis 25:11). It is a place of refuge, divine providence, and permanence of the chosen people in the promised land.
H0883.portee: This well reminds every reader that God sees our distress and our exile, even in a foreign land, and that He reveals Himself to those who cry out to Him. For Isaac and the patriarchs, it is a sign of the territory that God entrusts to them and of His faithful presence in the Negev.

sens: Fortified city in southern Israel, at the edge of the Negev desert
H0884.detail: 1. Beer-Sheba is a city located at the southern border of the territory of Israel, at the edge of the desert. Its name means "well of the oath" or "well of the seven," referring to a well and a solemn agreement made at this location. It is a major geographical and political landmark in the history of Israel.
H0884.origine: The Hebrew name בְּאֵר שֶׁבַע consists of "well" (bé'ér) and "oath" or "seven" (shéva). According to Genesis 21:31, the name comes from an oath made between Abraham and Abimelech regarding a well. This etymology anchors the place in patriarchal traditions and underscores the importance of covenants in biblical faith.
H0884.emploi: Beer-Sheba appears 33 times in the Bible, primarily in the Old Testament. It first appears in the story of Abraham and Hagar (Genesis 21:14), then in the story of Isaac (Genesis 26:23). It becomes an administrative and military landmark: the expression "from Dan to Beer-Sheba" designates the full extent of the territory of Israel from north to south (2 Samuel 17:11). The city is mentioned during royal tours (2 Chronicles 19:4) and in the context of censuses. It retains its importance even after the exile, as evidenced by its mention in Nehemiah. The prophets Amos criticize it as a site of idol worship (Amos 5:5; Amos 8:14).
H0884.portee: Beer-Sheba embodies the extent of the promise made to the patriarchs and the unity of the people of Israel under one government. For the Christian reader, this city serves as a reminder that God honors His covenants and that biblical geography tells the story of salvation. Its recurring importance highlights how God accompanies His people through generations, from the desert to established kingdoms.

sens: City in the territory of Benjamin, in the Old Testament
Inhabitant of this city
H0886.detail:
1. Beeroth is a city located in the territory of Benjamin, in the land of Israel. Its name means "the wells," which evokes the importance of water for the inhabitants of this region. The city is mentioned in the context of the early part of David's reign, particularly during the tragic events that follow the death of King Saul (2 Samuel 4:2).
2. The Beerothites are the inhabitants of this city. During the political turmoil after Saul's death, the Beerothites had to flee their city and take refuge in Gittaim, where they settled permanently (2 Samuel 4:3). Some of them later served David: thus Naharaï, from Beeroth, became the armor-bearer of Joab and was among David's warriors (2 Samuel 23:37).
H0886.origine: The name Beeroth comes from a Hebrew root meaning "wells" (in the plural). It is a geographical name that describes the characteristics of the place: an area where underground water was accessible and vital for the inhabitants. The demonym "Beerothite" designates someone from this city, following the common pattern of names of peoples and cities in Israel.
H0886.emploi: Beeroth and the Beerothites appear five times in the Bible, exclusively in 2 Samuel 4 and 23:37. The most detailed passage (2 Samuel 4:2-9) recounts how two sons of Rimmon of Beeroth, Rechab and Baanah, assassinated Ish-Bosheth, the son of Saul, which constitutes a bloody episode in the consolidation of David's power. These two men thought they were pleasing David by eliminating a rival, but David instead condemned them severely for this crime. Naharaï of Beeroth is also mentioned as one of the warriors in David's army (2 Samuel 23:37), showing that inhabitants of Beeroth integrated into the structures of the unified kingdom.

sens: To emit a foul odor, a stench
To become abominable, detestable in the eyes of others
To cause disgust or aversion
To lose all credit or esteem
H0887.detail:
1. Literally, the word describes the foul odor that emanates from something: the dead fish of the Nile that rot emit an unbearable stench (Exodus 7:18), or the food that remains rots and infests the place (Exodus 16:24).
2. Figuratively, the word depicts one who becomes odious, detestable in the eyes of others — like Jacob fearing that the massacre at Shechem would make him abominable to the Canaanites (Genesis 34:30), or David who pretends to have fallen into disgrace with Israel to better deceive King Achish (1 Samuel 27:12).
3. Sometimes the word expresses the action of deliberately disgusting: Absalom wants to make himself so odious to his father that all Israel will support him against him (2 Samuel 16:21).
4. The underlying image is that of moral decay or betrayal: to become foul in the eyes of others is to lose all credit and become despicable.
H0887.origine: The Hebrew root expresses the idea of a repulsive odor and a corruption that spreads. It is also used for moral abomination: one who stinks is one who is rejected. The image starts from the concrete — rotting flesh — to describe what is repugnant in relational and moral domains.
H0887.emploi: The verb appears sixteen times in the Hebrew text, especially in Exodus during the plagues (corrupted water, dead fish, spoiled food). But its major use is figurative: to describe one who becomes detestable in the eyes of a people or a leader. Jacob fears to stink in the eyes of the Canaanites (Genesis 34:30), David pretends to have become odious to Israel (1 Samuel 27:12), Absalom intends to make himself abominable to his father to galvanize popular support (2 Samuel 16:21). The word paints the sudden loss of credit or the deliberately provoked aversion.
H0887.portee: This word reminds us that reputation, integrity, and honor are fragile: one action can make you abominable in the eyes of an entire community. It also invites reflection on the seriousness of becoming odious through betrayal or impiety — a strong biblical image of distancing from God.

sens: To be in a troubled and painful heart disposition
To feel dissatisfaction or displeasure regarding a situation
To be deeply saddened by bad news
H0888.detail:
1. The word paints the inner state of a person shaken by news that wounds them. When King Darius learns that Daniel has been thrown into the lion's den due to a trap set for him, he is "very distressed" (Daniel 6:14): this is not simply a passing emotion, but a turmoil of the heart that drives him to act to save the one he values. The affliction here is mixed with regret and determination.
2. The word can also express a form of displeasure or dissatisfaction regarding something that is unsuitable, disturbing, or causes discomfort. It is a feeling that arises from an inner disturbance in the face of what is bad or undesirable.
H0888.origine: The Aramaic word בְּאֵשׁ (be.esh) comes from the root בָּאַשׁ (ba.ash, "stench"), which initially evokes an unpleasant and repulsive odor. Through natural semantic extension, what stinks becomes what is bad, what repels — first in a physical sense, then in a moral and emotional sense. The underlying idea is one of repugnance or aversion, hence the transition to "to be distressed" or "to be displeasing" at heart.
H0888.emploi: This word appears only once in biblical Aramaic, in Daniel 6:14, where it describes King Darius's reaction to the news that Daniel has been sentenced to death according to the law of the Medes and Persians. Although the king is in power, he discovers that he is trapped by his own edicts, and this situation deeply distresses him. The context shows that this is not a mere emotion, but an affliction that mobilizes him: he spends the night without sleeping, seeking to save Daniel at dawn.
H0888.portee: This affection reveals the king's conscience: despite his absolute authority, he recognizes that he has made a mistake in signing the edict, and he is distressed by the injustice he can no longer prevent. For the Christian reader, this passage shows how the heart can be stirred by injustice and error, and how sincere affliction can lead to seeking redemption and repair, even when circumstances seem insurmountable.

sens: Strong and unpleasant odor
Odor of death and decomposition
Sign of divine judgment and destruction
H0889.detail:
1. The word refers to a repugnant and suffocating odor: that which rises from decomposing corpses on the battlefield in Isaiah 34:3, or that which escapes from the fleeing army in Joel 2:20.
2. It specifically evokes the stench of death. When God judges nations, it is through plague, war, famine — all calamities that leave bodies, and with them this horrible odor that rises to heaven. In Amos 4:10, the corpses of young men struck by the plague even infect the camp of the survivors.
3. The stench becomes a symbol: it visibly and sensibly manifests God's anger. It does not escape discreetly; it "rises in the air" (Joel 2:20), scandalous and impossible to ignore, just like divine judgment itself.
H0889.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of decay and infection. It is a concrete term that paints the image of what decomposes and becomes repugnant. In biblical Hebrew, words with similar meanings express physical corruption and, by extension, moral or spiritual defilement.
H0889.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Bible, always in a context of divine judgment: twice in Joel to describe the fleeing of the locust army, and once in Amos to evoke the consequences of the plague. Each time, it underscores the horror and extent of the punishment: not only are the enemies defeated or the people struck, but the ruin is so total, so repugnant, that it offends the nostrils of all. It is a realistic and overwhelming detail.
H0889.portee: This word teaches the reader that God's judgment is not a distant abstraction: it has visible, tangible, and sensible consequences. The stench rising from battlefields or infected camps is the sign that the divine word is being fulfilled. It also invites one to take the prophetic warning seriously: not returning to God exposes one to consequences whose horror cannot be ignored.

sens: foul or toxic weed
weed that grows among food crops
plant harmful to the harvest
H0890.detail:
1. The tares refer to a foul-smelling or tasting weed, likely toxic or dangerous for livestock. The Hebrew word specifically evokes something that stinks or harms.
2. It is an undesirable weed that grows spontaneously in cultivated fields, among wheat and barley. It competes with the true crops and chokes them. In Job 31:40, Job curses his field wishing that the tares completely cover it instead of yielding a beautiful harvest: this is the height of waste and curse.
H0890.origine: The Hebrew word ba'sha comes from a root meaning "to stink" or "to be bad." The tares thus carry the idea of something repugnant, corrupt. It is a plant whose bad nature — both in appearance and effect — is evident.
H0890.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Job 31:40. Job lists the curses he deserves if his actions are dishonest: he wishes that his field, instead of producing useful grain, be overrun by thorns and tares. This personal imprecation illustrates the biblical idea that sin sterilizes and destroys what one possesses, turning blessing into curse.
H0890.portee: The tares symbolize in this verse the natural consequence of injustice: the guilty heart carries within it a corruption that extends to all it touches, including its possessions. For the Christian reader, this text reminds that only moral integrity and justice produce a fruitful life; in contrast, sin generates only disorder and destruction.

sens: Grapes of poor quality, sour or inedible, that a vine produces instead of good fruit
Figuratively, disappointing or undesirable result
H0891.detail:
1. In common language, this word refers to very poor quality grapes — sour, barren, or rotten — that the vine produces instead of the beautiful fruits expected. In Isaiah 5:2, the vineyard owner carefully plants a "delightful vine" and expects good grapes, but harvests "bad" grapes instead.
2. Figuratively and prophetically, the term evokes complete failure, the bitter disappointment of the divine plan. When God says in Isaiah 5:4, "Why, when I expected it to produce good grapes, did it produce bad?" he speaks of the people of Israel who, despite all divine care, produce not justice and righteousness, but injustice and evil.
H0891.origine: The Hebrew word originally evokes something stinking or repulsive ("stinkberries" or "stinking grapes"), hence the idea of rotten and inedible fruits. Its primary image — grapes that stink and are worthless — makes it perfect for describing not only agricultural failure but also moral and spiritual rejection.
H0891.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both in the famous parable of the vineyard in Isaiah 5. God, who has prepared everything for Israel to be a beautiful productive vineyard, finds instead sour or rotten grapes — an eloquent image of the people's unfaithfulness. It is a prophetic word of judgment, not on an accidental failure, but on a deliberate refusal to bear good fruit.
H0891.portee: This image reminds us that God expects from his people, and from each of us, fruit that corresponds to the care and grace he gives us. The "bad grapes" are not the absence of fruit, but spoiled, unworthy fruit — which is worse. It is a call to produce a righteous and holy life, in accordance with God's benevolent intention toward us.

sens: The pupil, the black and sensitive part at the center of the eye
What is most precious, most dear, most jealously guarded
H0892.detail:
1. The apple of the eye is the pupil, the small black disc at the center of the eye through which light enters: it is the most delicate and sensitive part of the eye, the one that is instinctively protected. Zechariah 2:8 literally speaks of the apple of God's eye to designate what is most vulnerable and precious to him.

2. By extension, the apple of the eye becomes an image of what is infinitely dear, jealously protected: for one tolerates no aggression against one's pupil. In Zechariah 2:8, God says that whoever touches Israel touches the apple of his eye — in other words, he attacks what God cherishes most, which he fiercely defends.
H0892.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that likely means "pupil" or "daughter" (Hebrew sometimes calls the pupil "the daughter of the eye"). The image is very concrete: the pupil shines and reflects the image of the one who looks, like a little girl, hence this tender name. This term illustrates how the Hebrews named things according to what they evoked for them.
H0892.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Zechariah 2:8, where it expresses God's jealous love for his people. God says that Israel is the apple of his eye — something that cannot be touched without punishment. This unique usage shows the importance of this image to express the most intense divine attachment: that which protects what is most vulnerable and most precious.
H0892.portee: This expression reveals God's heart toward his people: Israel is not merely a possession, but the object of extreme tenderness and vigilance. For every Christian, it affirms that whoever believes in God is also precious in his sight, deserving the same jealous protection. It invites recognition of the infinite value that each person has before God.

sens: A man who lived during the time of exile and return
A family leader among the exiles who returned to Jerusalem
H0893G.detail:
1. Bebai is a man mentioned for the first time in the list of exiles who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem (Ezra 2:11). His name also designates his family: he is the head of a household whose descendants formed an important clan among the restored people.

2. Bebai appears at the head of several genealogical lists of the return from exile. He is presented as a respected family leader: his descendants were quite numerous (six hundred twenty-three at the initial return, according to Ezra 2:11, and six hundred twenty-eight according to the parallel in Nehemiah 7:16), and some of his sons held specific responsibilities, such as Zechariah who accompanied Ezra (Ezra 8:11) or Johanan who participated in the decisions of the restored people (Ezra 10:28).
H0893G.origine: The name literally means "my cavities" in Hebrew. Although the exact etymology remains debated, the name may evoke a physical characteristic or a poetic image. Bebai is a typical patronymic from the context of the Babylonian exile, borne by several members of his family who played a role in the restoration of Jerusalem.
H0893G.emploi: Bebai is mentioned four times in the Bible, all in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah. He first appears in the register of families who returned from Babylon under the leadership of Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:11). His name reappears in the parallel list in the book of Nehemiah (7:16) with a slightly different number of descendants. Ezra 8:11 mentions him through his son Zechariah, who represented the family before Ezra. Finally, Ezra 10:28 cites several of his sons among those who had married foreign women and had to renounce them. These references show that Bebai's family maintained a stable and respected place in the restored community.
H0893G.portee: The name of Bebai reminds the reader that God has not forgotten His people in exile and that He has restored them. These genealogical lists, seemingly dry, testify to God's faithfulness to His promises and the concrete reality of the return. They also show that the renewal of Jerusalem was built on ordinary families who, despite their weaknesses and mistakes (such as the mixed marriages reported in Ezra 10), participated in the reconstruction of God's people.

sens: Family leader during the return from exile after Babylon
H0893H.detail: Bebai is a man who figures among the leaders of the families of the exile during the return to Judea. He is mentioned in Ezra 8:11, where he is presented as the father of Zechariah and as a household leader whose one hundred twenty-three descendants return to Jerusalem under Ezra's leadership. He is an example of those Jewish families who preserved their identity during captivity and who take the lead in returning to the promised land.
H0893H.origine: The name Bebai literally means "my cavities" or "my hollows," an image that may evoke the idea of voids or hollows to be filled. This Hebrew name is characteristic of family names from this period of return from exile, borne by the ancestors of the Judean clans who reconstitute the community.
H0893H.emploi: Bebai appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 8:11. He is cited as the father of Zechariah and as a household leader whose descendants (one hundred twenty-three people according to the previous mention of the genealogy of the exiles) return with Ezra to Jerusalem. This context of the return from exile (around 458 B.C.) makes Bebai a representative of families that survived deportation and play a crucial role in the restoration of the Jewish community in Judea.

sens: Leader of the exiles who returned to Jerusalem
H0893I.detail: Bebai is a leader of the exiles who left Babylon to return to Jerusalem after the decree of Cyrus. He is among the signatories of the covenant made under Nehemiah's leadership to commit to observing the Law of Moses (Nehemiah 10:15). His name appears only once in the Bible, among the list of religious and civil leaders who sealed this solemn pact.
H0893I.origine: The name Bebai literally means "my cavities" in Hebrew, probably an image evoking hollows or pits. Although the precise meaning of the name is uncertain, it reflects Hebrew naming practices that often root in natural images or circumstances of birth.
H0893I.emploi: Bebai is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 10:15. He appears in the context of the restoration of the Jewish people after the Babylonian exile, alongside other leaders like Bunni and Azgad. These men represent the spiritual and civil elite of the repatriates, tasked with leading the community in its commitment to uphold the covenant with God. His status as a "leader" indicates that he held recognized authority among the returnees.

sens: The great capital of the ancient Babylonian empire, located on the Euphrates
The political and military power that dominates the Near East during the time of Judah's captivity
A symbol of wealth, power, and oppression against God's people
H0894.detail:
1. Babylon is the historical and political capital of the Babylonian empire, a major center of ancient civilization located on the banks of the Euphrates (in present-day Iraq). It is mentioned in Genesis as a city founded by Nimrod (Genesis 10:10), and its Hebrew name evokes the idea of confusion — recalling the confusion of languages at Babel (Genesis 11:9).

2. In Jeremiah's time, Babylon becomes the center of a formidable military empire that dominates the nations of the Middle East. Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, imposes his yoke on many kingdoms, and anyone who refuses "to submit their neck to the yoke of the king of Babylon" will be punished by sword, famine, and pestilence (Jeremiah 27:8).

3. For Judah, Babylon represents captivity and divine judgment: Jeremiah announces that the inhabitants of Jerusalem will be deported to Babylon (Jeremiah 20:4-5), which is fulfilled when Nebuchadnezzar destroys the Temple and exports the royal treasure (2 Chronicles 36:18; Ezra 1:11). It is a symbol of exile and separation from the promised land.

4. The prophets against Babylon (notably Isaiah 47 and Jeremiah 50-51) describe it as proud, wealthy, and corrupt, destined for divine destruction. The people in Babylon languish far from Jerusalem: Psalm 137:1 shows the exiles sitting by the rivers of Babylon, weeping for Zion.
H0894.origine: The Hebrew name בָּבֶל (Babel/Babylon) literally means "confusion by mixing" or "gate of God" according to interpretations. It is associated with the event of the Tower of Babel (Genesis 11:9), where God confuses the languages of men. Historically, the Akkadian name Babylon meant "gate of God," but the Bible plays on the phonetic similarity with the Hebrew בָּלַל (balal, "to mix"), which emphasizes the idea of divine confusion. This etymological link enriches the biblical symbolism of the name.
H0894.emploi: Babylon appears more than two hundred times in the Bible. It first designates an ancient city mentioned as early as Genesis, then becomes the center of the Neo-Babylonian empire (6th century B.C.) that threatens and then conquers Judah. In the historical books (2 Kings, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah), Babylon is the place from which the military threat originates, where the Judeans are deported, and where the treasures of the Temple are kept — but also from where the exiles return. In the prophets (particularly Jeremiah and Isaiah), Babylon becomes a figure of arrogant power that God will judge and destroy. In the Psalms (137), it is the place of exile and mourning for the Judeans far from Zion.
H0894.portee: Babylon teaches the reader that no human empire, no matter how powerful, escapes God's judgment. It also shows that even captivity and exile do not mean the end of divine promise: the exiles can return (Ezra 1:11), and God remains faithful to His people. It is a call not to place trust in the powers of the world, but to wait for the salvation of the Lord.

sens: The ancient capital of the Babylonian empire, a world power of the Middle East
The province or administrative region governed from Babylon
The political and cultural center where royal authority was exercised
The place of captivity and exile for the people of Judah
H0895.detail:
1. Babylon is the great ancient city built on the Euphrates, the capital of the Babylonian empire that dominated the Middle East. It is a powerful metropolis, residence of kings like Nebuchadnezzar (Ezra 5:12). It represents a world power and organized authority, capable of conquest and governance.

2. The word also refers to the entire administrative province or region under Babylonian control. Daniel receives the stewardship of the province of Babylon, showing that the term includes not only the city but an entire region (Daniel 2:49, 3:30).

3. Babylon is the seat of royal power and government. It is where the king's court, palaces, royal treasures are located, and from where decisions affecting the subjugated peoples are made (Ezra 7:16, Daniel 2:18).

4. For Israel, Babylon is primarily the place of exile: it is where Nebuchadnezzar took the captive people of Judah and from where King Cyrus would allow their return (Ezra 5:12, 5:17). It symbolizes deportation and separation from the promised land.
H0895.origine: The name means "confusion (by mixing)" in Hebrew and Aramaic, likely referring to the Tower of Babel built by men in this land — the same root as "to mix" or "to confuse." The name may also evoke "gate of the god" in Akkadian (Bab-ilu). The historical city was indeed on the Tigris and Euphrates, the center of Mesopotamian civilization.
H0895.emploi: The word "Babylon" appears about 25 times in the Bible, concentrated in the books of Ezra and Daniel, both of which recount the captivity and events after the exile. In the provided usages, Babylon is first the seat of Nebuchadnezzar who conquers Jerusalem and takes the people captive (Ezra 5:12). It is then the province where the exiled Jews live and where men like Daniel and his companions obtain positions of authority (Daniel 2:49, 3:30). The king of Babylon receives his wise men there and makes his decisions (Daniel 2:18, 2:24). The royal treasures of Babylon are used to finance the reconstruction of the temple (Ezra 7:16). Babylon embodies both oppression (the captivity) and, gradually, a place where God protects His people and where exiles serve faithfully.
H0895.portee: For the Christian reader, Babylon reminds us that the sins of the fathers have serious consequences — the destruction of the temple and the exile (Ezra 5:12). But it also teaches that God never loses control: even in the heart of an enemy power, He protects His people and elevates them to places of honor (Daniel 2:49, 3:30). The exile to Babylon is not the final word: God allows for the return and restoration of the temple. It is a lesson on divine judgment, persistent grace, and the hope that remains even in the darkest trials.

sens: inhabitant or official of Babylon
related to Babylon or its traditions
person from a region of the Babylonian empire
H0896.detail:
1. The word designates an inhabitant or official of Babylon (the great city of Mesopotamia) or of its empire. In Ezra 4:9, it lists the peoples and officials from various regions of the Persian empire who oppose the reconstruction of the temple: the Babylonian is associated with other ethnic groups from this vast territory conquered by Persia.
2. More broadly, the word can refer to anything related to Babylon: its inhabitants, its administration, its traditions. It is a way to characterize the peoples who lived in the ancient Babylonian territory under Persian domination.
3. In the context of Ezra, the term helps to show the diversity of peoples and opponents: they are not only Babylonians, but representatives from several regions of the vast Persian empire who seek to block the work.
H0896.origine: The word comes from Babylon (בָּבֶל, Babel in Hebrew), whose name means "confusion" or "mixing" — an allusion to the famous Tower of Babel and the confusion of languages (Genesis 11). The adjective Babylonian was thus formed from this proper name to designate what belongs to this region or to those who came from it. For the Hebrews, Babylon was the great imperial power that had deported them (587 B.C.), hence a strong historical and symbolic charge.
H0896.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezra 4:9. In this verse, it is part of a list of peoples and officials from the various provinces of the Persian empire who together write a letter to the king to oppose the reconstruction of the temple. The context is that of the obstacles faced by the Jews returned from exile to rebuild Jerusalem. This unique occurrence shows that the term was used to identify the ethnic or administrative groups of the vast Babylonian territory that became a Persian province.
H0896.portee: This word reminds the reader of the reality of Israel's dispersion and foreign domination: even after the exile, the Judeans must face opponents from the peoples who once defeated them. It is also a sign that the restoration of Jerusalem did not happen without difficulty, and that the people had to rely on divine protection to overcome these external obstacles.

sens: to act disloyally, to fail in fidelity towards someone or an engagement
to show infidelity in a covenant, contract, or relationship
to strip, plunder violently
to commit an offense, a betrayal by word or deed
H0898.detail:
1. To act disloyally and fail in fidelity: this is the fundamental meaning of the word, that of breaking a promise or commitment to someone. When one betrays, one abandons the one to whom one was supposed to remain faithful. Jeremiah denounces Israel: "The house of Israel and the house of Judah have been unfaithful to me" (Jeremiah 5:11).
2. To show infidelity towards a covenant or contract: more specifically, it is to violate a solemnly established relationship, like the people who transgress the covenant made with God. Hosea states clearly: "They, like Adam, have transgressed the covenant; there they have been unfaithful to me" (Hosea 6:7).
3. To strip, plunder: the word also takes on the meaning of seizing, stealing by force. In the context of destruction and divine judgment, we see the "plunderers" who "plunder" (Isaiah 24:16), using the same root to designate both the one who betrays and the one who devastates.
4. To commit an offense or betrayal by word: it is to betray by what one says. The psalmist refuses to "betray the descendants of your children" by speaking against the people of God (Psalms 73:15).
H0898.origine: The Hebrew verb comes from a root that expresses the idea of breaking, violating, acting disloyally. Its basic image is that of a traitor who abandons: in the Old Testament, this word appears mainly to describe Israel's infidelity to the covenant with the Lord, or more generally the breaking of an established trust. The root carries the idea of violence and treachery.
H0898.emploi: This verb appears 39 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Psalms, Proverbs, Jeremiah, and the minor prophets. It is used in three main contexts. First, infidelity in the covenant with God: Israel has betrayed the Lord by abandoning its commitment to Him (Jeremiah 5:11, Hosea 6:7, Malachi 2:10-16). Next, disloyalty between people: a friend who cannot be counted on to be faithful (Job 6:15, Psalms 25:3), an unfaithful wife (Jeremiah 3:20), a treacherous companion (Judges 9:23). Finally, pillaging and violent theft, where the traitor becomes one who devastates (Isaiah 24:16, Isaiah 33:1). The moral contexts clearly indicate that betrayal produces serious consequences.
H0898.portee: This word reminds the Christian of the seriousness of infidelity towards God and towards others. It emphasizes that betrayal is not a fleeting weakness, but a breaking of covenant that wounds the established relationship. At the same time, by showing how God Himself denounces this sin, it invites vigilance: not betraying the trust placed in us is to honor our commitment to God and others. It is a call to true faithfulness.

sens: act of betraying, failing in loyalty
traitorous behavior, infidelity towards God or someone
H0899A.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the act of betraying, violating trust. In Isaiah 24:16, the context of the plunderers who "are relentless" in their looting evokes the idea of people acting violently and without respect for rules, betraying the established order. It is an act of rupture, of fraud.
2. In a broader and spiritual sense, it refers to infidelity towards God or towards a commitment made. In Jeremiah 12:1, the "treacherous" (literally "the traitors") are those who live in peace while they should be punished for their infidelity to the divine covenant. The prophet is astonished that the wicked prosper despite their betrayal of God's justice.
H0899A.origine: The Hebrew word בגד comes from a root that evokes the idea of turning away, betraying trust. It belongs to the family of words expressing treachery and disloyalty. The fundamental meaning is one who "turns against" the one who believed or loved them.
H0899A.emploi: This word appears twice in the provided passages. In Isaiah 24:16, in a context of divine judgment on the earth, it describes the violent actions of plunderers who act without restraint. In Jeremiah 12:1, it qualifies the "treacherous" or "traitors" who prosper despite their infidelity towards God. In both cases, the word refers to a violation of loyalty or justice, either towards the established order or towards God Himself.
H0899A.portee: This word invites the believer to be vigilant against betrayal and disloyalty towards God. It also reminds that the infidelity of traitors does not escape God's notice, even when they temporarily prosper: God sees and will judge. It is a call to faithfulness and trust in divine justice, even when it seems delayed.

sens: Piece of fabric or leather worn on the body for covering or protection
Complete outfit or costume, set of clothing
Household linen, fabric intended to cover or drape
Figuratively, an envelope that covers or can be consumed
H0899B.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a garment in the concrete sense: anything worn for covering. It is given as a gift (Genesis 24:53, where the servant offers garments to Rebekah), changed to present oneself properly (Genesis 27:15, where Rebekah prepares clothes for Jacob), and washed after contact with the unclean (Leviticus 11:28).
2. The word also encompasses clothing in a broader sense, the entirety of a person's attire. The priestly garments of the high priest (Leviticus 16:23) constitute his uniform as a minister of worship — these specialized garments cannot be worn anywhere.
3. It can refer to linen, particularly fabrics that cover objects or bodies. In Leviticus, it speaks of the garment where leprosy may appear (Leviticus 13:47-59), showing that the word applies to any fabric.
4. Figuratively, the garment becomes an image: in Isaiah 50:9, God's just ones will fall "in tatters like a garment" that the moth will devour, a vivid comparison of total and inevitable destruction.
H0899B.origine: The Hebrew word בֶּגֶד comes from a root that fundamentally means "to cover" or "to clothe." It is a very common term in ancient Hebrew, attested from the earliest books of the Bible. It does not have significant morphological variants: it is mostly encountered in singular and plural forms in contexts as diverse as everyday life (the garment of an adulterous woman), worship (the priest's garments), or ritual hygiene (impurity contracted by contact with a corpse).
H0899B.emploi: The word appears 188 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in Genesis and Leviticus. In Genesis, it designates the garments given as gifts or worn to deceive (Rebekah gives her elder son's clothes to Jacob). Leviticus frequently uses the word to speak of ritual impurity contracted by garments (one who touches a corpse must wash their garments), of leprosy that can affect a garment (entire chapters deal with the diagnosis of the disease in linen), and of specialized garments for worship (the linen garments of the high priest). In historical narratives (2 Kings), torn garments express mourning or distress (Eliakim tears his garments upon learning of the Assyrian threat). Isaiah uses it figuratively to evoke wear and destruction.
H0899B.portee: For the believer, this word reminds that clothing is not a luxury but a necessity, and that the Lord pays attention to it: He covers our nakedness from the very beginning. It also emphasizes the importance of acts of purity and respect towards God: washing one's garments after impurity expresses the restoration of the relationship with Him. Finally, resonating with prophetic imagery, it teaches us that all earthly things, even what covers and protects us, are destined to pass away.

sens: City of the tribe of Dan, located in the territory of Judah
Place of origin of Samson and his parents
H0847.detail:
1. Eschthaol is a city that belongs to the tribe of Dan, situated in the mountainous and fertile region of the territory of Judah, near Zorah (Joshua 15:33 and 19:41). It is an important urban center in this area, from which warriors and explorers set out.
2. Eschthaol is the place where Samson grew up: it is between Zorah and Eschthaol that the Spirit of the Lord began to stir him, and it is there that Samson was buried after his death, in the tomb of his father Manoah (Judges 13:25 and 16:31).
H0847.origine: The name means "supplication" or "entreaty" in Hebrew, perhaps reflecting a pious significance. It is a Canaanite city that the tribe of Dan occupied during the conquest of the land.
H0847.emploi: Eschthaol appears seven times in the Bible, exclusively in the Old Testament. It is first mentioned as one of the cities in the territory of Dan at the time of the division of the promised land (Joshua 15:33; 19:41). It then significantly reappears in the story of Samson: it is the starting point of the tribe of Dan's explorations to find new territory (Judges 18:2, 8), and it is between Zorah and Eschthaol that Samson spent his childhood and where he was buried (Judges 13:25; 16:31). The city thus serves as a geographical setting for one of the greatest figures of the Old Testament.
H0847.portee: Eschthaol reminds us that God places His servants in concrete contexts: Samson is not a hero detached from the world, but a man rooted in his community, family, and territory. It is a call to see how God works through the ordinary places of our lives.
